lessons.title: Who may make which law: the federal bargain
lessons.summary: Malaysia has two kinds of law-maker, and each is given its own list of subjects. The Ninth Schedule holds the lists, and Article 75 says what happens when the two collide.

sections.keypoint: Two law-makers share one country, and each may only legislate on its own list.

body.text: Malaysia has two kinds of law-maker. Parliament makes law for the whole country. Each State has its own assembly, which makes law for that State alone.
Neither one can make law about anything it likes. Each is given a list of subjects, and a law outside its own list is invalid however sensible it may be.

Imagine the Selangor assembly passed a law setting the punishment for theft. It would be void. Criminal law belongs to Parliament and not to a State, so every member of the assembly could vote for it and it would still be worth nothing.
Where do the lists come from? The Constitution sets them out, and Article 74 says who may use which of them.
Parliament may make laws with respect to matters in the Federal List and the Concurrent List; a State Legislature may make laws with respect to matters in the State List and the Concurrent List.
body.source: Federal Constitution Arts 74(1) and 74(2), read with the Ninth Schedule

body.text: Put simply: Parliament works from the Federal List and the Concurrent List, and a State works from the State List and the Concurrent List. The three lists are printed in the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution.

List I is the Federal List, List II is the State List, and List III is the Concurrent List, which both of them may use. Sabah and Sarawak also have supplementary lists of their own, because they joined the federation on their own terms.

sections.keypoint: The Ninth Schedule's three lists — and land is a State matter while criminal law is federal.

body.text: The Ninth Schedule sets out three lists. One says what Parliament may make law about. One says what a State may. The third says what both may. The table is the outline — the Schedule itself runs much longer.

body.prompt: Land is on the State List. So who made the National Land Code, the Act that decides how a lot in Kedah is transferred?
options: The Kedah legislature, since land is a State subject
Parliament, with each State adopting it
Both together, because land is on the Concurrent List
body.reveal: Parliament made it. Article 76 lets Parliament legislate on a State subject so that the law can be uniform. Such a law takes effect in a State when that State adopts it. If you picked the first answer, that is the ordinary reading of the lists, and it is why this one has to be learned as an exception.

body.text: Here is the counter-intuitive one. Land is a State subject, yet the National Land Code is a federal Act. Article 76 is what allows that: it lets Parliament legislate on a State subject so that the law can be uniform across the country. Such a law takes effect in a State only when that State's legislature adopts it. The Code covers the Peninsula, while Sabah and Sarawak have land laws of their own. If you cannot explain that, the land material later will not make sense.

Puan Salmah buys a lot in Kedah. The rules for getting her name onto the title come from a federal Act, the National Land Code. Land is still a State subject. Article 76 is the bridge between those two facts.

body.caption: The three lists, in outline
rows: Civil and criminal law and procedure
Protection of wild animals and birds
body.note: Note the two counter-intuitive entries. **Land** is a State matter, which is why a federal National Land Code needs Art 76 to explain it; **criminal law** is federal, which is why the Penal Code is national.

sections.keypoint: Where valid laws collide, federal wins and the State law is void only so far as it clashes.

body.text: Sometimes both law-makers have acted and the two laws do not agree. Encik Rahim needs a licence, and each law sets a different condition for getting one. He cannot obey both of them.
The Constitution settles that contest in a single sentence.
If any State law is inconsistent with a federal law, the federal law shall prevail and the State law shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void.
Put simply: the federal law wins. But only the clashing part of the State law dies. The rest of the State law stands, and severing the bad part is the ordinary course.
There is also an earlier question, and it is the one people skip. Article 75 assumes that the federal law is itself a valid one.
A federal Act on a State subject prevails over nothing at all. It is void itself, under Article 4(1).

A State enactment on the licensing of a trade collides with a federal statute doing the same thing. Do not begin by asking which one wins. Begin by asking whether trade and commerce is a federal subject at all. Only if the federal law is valid does Article 75 do any work.

body.title: The order the questions come in

items.text: Was the subject within the legislature's list at all? A law outside it is void under Art 4(1), and Art 75 never arises.
If both laws are valid and they collide, Art 75 makes the federal law prevail.
The State law is void only to the extent of the inconsistency. Severance is the ordinary course, not striking the whole enactment.

body.q: A federal Act and a State enactment cover the same ground and contradict each other. Which question comes first?
options: Whether the federal law was within Parliament's power at all
Which of the two was passed later
Whether the federal law prevails under Article 75
body.why: Article 75 assumes the federal law is a valid one. A federal Act on a State subject, with nothing in the Constitution allowing it, is void under Article 4(1). A void law prevails over nothing. Reaching for Article 75 first skips a whole argument.

sections.keypoint: The Constitution outranks both, and a later inconsistent law is void to that extent.
sections.h: The Constitution is the higher law

body.text: Why can a court say that a law passed by Parliament is worth nothing? Because one law sits above all the others.
This Constitution is the supreme law of the Federation and any law passed after Merdeka Day which is inconsistent with this Constitution shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void.
Put simply: the Constitution beats every other law, and anything inconsistent with it is void so far as it is inconsistent.

In some countries Parliament may pass whatever it likes, and no court may say otherwise. Not here. In Malaysia a court can be asked whether the law-maker had the power at all, and that is the first question about any statute.

There are rules about *how* you may attack a law on that ground. Articles 4(3) and 4(4) restrict it, and proceedings in the Federal Court need leave — the court's permission to bring the case at all. Check the current text and the current practice before saying how such a challenge must be started. This is a procedural trap rather than a substantive one, and it catches people who have the law right.

sections.keypoint: Ask who had power to pass the law before asking whether the law is fair — it often ends there.

body.text: Suppose a new law limits what people may say at a gathering. The instinct is to ask whether the limit is a fair one, and whether Article 10 permits it.
Stop one step earlier than that. Ask whether the law-maker could pass such a law at all. If it could not, the law is dead, and Article 10 is never reached.

So the order runs: power first, then whether the content is constitutional, then what the words of the provision mean. An answer that goes straight to proportionality has skipped a complete and often decisive argument.

quiz.q: Federal law beats State law where the two clash. Which Article says so?
options: Art 4(1)
Art 75
Art 74
Art 76
quiz.why: Art 75. The State law is void only so far as it clashes, and the rest of it survives.

quiz.q: Land is a State subject, yet the National Land Code is a federal Act. What makes that possible?
options: Art 76, which lets Parliament legislate on State subjects for uniformity
Art 75, because federal law prevails
Art 4(1) supremacy
Land is in fact on the Federal List
quiz.why: Art 76 is the uniformity route, and such a law takes effect in a State only when that State adopts it.

quiz.q: Parliament passes an Act on a subject that is on the State List. What is the position?
options: It prevails under Art 75
It is valid but unenforceable
It is valid if the State consents afterwards
It is invalid; Art 75 never arises
quiz.why: Art 75 assumes a valid federal law. Power is the earlier question, and Art 4(1) answers it.
quiz.source: Federal Constitution Art 4(1); Ninth Schedule List II

quiz.q: Which of these is a State subject?
options: Criminal law and procedure
Islamic law and Malay custom
Citizenship
External affairs
quiz.why: List II holds Islamic law, the personal and family law of Muslims, Malay custom, land and local government.
quiz.source: Federal Constitution, Ninth Schedule List II

quiz.q: What does Art 4(1) say?
options: Parliament is sovereign
The Constitution is supreme, and inconsistent law is void to that extent
Federal law prevails over State law
The courts may not review legislation
quiz.why: Supremacy is what makes an argument about legislative power available at all.

quiz.q: In a fundamental liberties problem, what should you check before asking whether a limit is proportionate?
options: Whether the plaintiff has standing
Whether the case is reported
Whether the restriction is popular
Whether the law-maker had power to pass the law at all
quiz.why: A limit imposed by a law nobody had power to pass fails before Art 10 is ever reached.

lessons.title: Judicial power, Article 121, and the basic structure argument
lessons.summary: In 1988 the words vesting judicial power in the courts were taken out of Article 121(1). What survived that amendment is still one of the live questions in Malaysian constitutional law.

sections.keypoint: A court's power to decide your case comes from somewhere, and in 1988 that somewhere was rewritten.

body.text: A court's power to decide your case has to come from somewhere. Where it comes from was changed in 1988, and lawyers are still arguing about what that change did.

Before 1988, Article 121(1) provided that the judicial power of the Federation was vested in two High Courts and in the lower courts. Judicial power means the power to decide disputes and to say what the law is.

The amendment replaced that formula. The Article now says the courts shall have such jurisdiction and powers as may be conferred by or under federal law. Jurisdiction means the range of matters a court is allowed to deal with.

On one reading that made the courts' jurisdiction entirely a creature of statute. On another, judicial power is inherent in a constitution that separates the branches, and deleting the sentence that describes it cannot take it away.
Malaysian courts have taken both views.

body.title: What the 1988 amendment did to Article 121(1)
body.caption: The argument is about what the replacement left behind. Do not state either reading as settled; find the most recent Federal Court authority before you write about it.
body.alt: Three points. Before 1988, Article 121(1) vested the judicial power of the Federation in the two High Courts and the courts below them. In 1988 that formula was replaced, so the courts have such jurisdiction and powers as federal law confers. Since then Malaysian courts have taken both readings: jurisdiction as a creature of statute, and judicial power as inherent in the Constitution.

events.label: Judicial power vested in the courts
The formula is replaced
events.note: such jurisdiction as federal law confers

events.label: Both readings taken
events.note: creature of statute, or inherent power

body.text: This is a moving area, and that is exactly why it is written about so often. Do not state either reading as settled law. Find the most recent Federal Court authority before you rely on one.

sections.keypoint: Article 121(1A) takes matters within Syariah jurisdiction away from the civil courts.

body.text: Malaysia has civil courts and it has Syariah courts. The Syariah courts are State courts, set up by State law, and they deal with Islamic law matters concerning Muslims.
What happens when one dispute could belong to either system? A clause added in 1988 answers part of that question.
The courts referred to in Clause (1) shall have no jurisdiction in respect of any matter within the jurisdiction of the Syariah courts.
Put simply: where a matter is within Syariah jurisdiction, the civil courts must keep out of it.

body.prompt: Clause (1A) takes a class of matters away from the civil courts. Before you read on — what does it give the Syariah courts?
options: Jurisdiction over Islamic law matters
Nothing — it only removes power from the civil courts
The final say in any dispute involving a Muslim
body.reveal: It gives them nothing. Taking power away from one court is not the same as handing it to another. The Syariah courts get their jurisdiction from State enactments made under List II. That is why the first question in these cases is what the State law actually covers.

body.text: Now read the clause again for what it does not do. It is not a grant of power to the Syariah courts. Their own jurisdiction comes from State enactments made under List II.
That distinction matters. If the matter is outside Syariah jurisdiction, clause (1A) does nothing at all, and the civil court keeps its power.

A man dies and his family disagree about who should bury him, and by what rites. Or a marriage ends, one parent converts, and both go to court over a child. One dispute can have a civil side and a Syariah side. These are the hardest cases, and they usually turn on how the question is characterised rather than on any disagreement about the rule.

sections.keypoint: Could Parliament amend away judicial review itself? That is the basic structure argument.

body.text: Parliament can amend the Constitution. Suppose it amended away the courts' power to review anything at all. Could it?

The basic structure argument says no. Certain features are so fundamental that they cannot be removed even by an amendment passed in the proper way. Judicial power, the rule of law and the separation of powers are the usual candidates.
The idea began in India. It has been received in Malaysia unevenly.

The Malaysian position has changed direction more than once. There are Federal Court decisions rejecting the doctrine and later ones applying it. If you write about this, write about the sequence and its current state, and give the citations. An assertion here with no case name is worth nothing.

The practical use of the doctrine is narrow. It is an argument of last resort against a constitutional amendment, and not a general licence to strike down ordinary legislation. Confusing those two is the commonest error made with it.

body.q: What does the basic structure argument claim?
options: That the Constitution cannot be amended
That some features cannot be removed, even by a properly passed amendment
That a law inconsistent with the Constitution is void
body.why: It is an argument about the limits of the power to amend. The last answer is Article 4(1), which is settled and is a different point. Treating the doctrine as a general licence to strike down ordinary legislation is the commonest error made with it.

sections.keypoint: Constitutional questions have their own forum, and getting it wrong is not a small mistake.

body.text: Forum means which court hears the matter. On constitutional questions the Constitution is specific about it.

items: Only the Federal Court may determine whether a law made by Parliament or a State Legislature is invalid because it relates to a matter outside legislative competence.
The Federal Court also determines disputes between two States, or between the Federation and a State.
A constitutional question arising in the High Court may be referred up to the Federal Court. The Constitution and the Courts of Judicature Act 1964 set out the mechanism and its limits.

body.text: Getting the forum wrong wastes the case. An answer that reaches the right constitutional conclusion in the wrong court has not advised the client at all.

body.title: Which court hears a constitutional question
body.caption: Forum is decided by the kind of question, not by where the dispute started. A High Court cannot pronounce a statute invalid on the ground that it was beyond legislative power.
body.alt: A question about the kind of constitutional question, branching three ways. Whether a law made by Parliament or a State Legislature is invalid: only the Federal Court may determine it. A dispute between two States, or between the Federation and a State: the Federal Court. A constitutional question arising in the High Court: it may be referred up to the Federal Court.
body.question: What kind of constitutional question is it?

branches.cond: State v State, or Federation v State
branches.label: Federal Court

quiz.q: What did the 1988 amendment do to Art 121(1)?
options: Vested judicial power in Parliament
Replaced the vesting of judicial power with jurisdiction conferred by federal law
Abolished appeals to the Privy Council
Created the Court of Appeal
quiz.why: The vesting words went out and a conferral formula came in. What that did is still argued about.

quiz.q: What does Art 121(1A) do?
options: Grants jurisdiction to the Syariah courts
Makes Syariah courts superior courts
Removes civil court jurisdiction over matters within Syariah jurisdiction
Creates a right of appeal to the Federal Court
quiz.why: It subtracts jurisdiction from the civil courts. It grants the Syariah courts nothing; their power comes from State enactments.

quiz.q: A matter falls outside Syariah jurisdiction. What follows for Art 121(1A)?
options: The civil court still has no jurisdiction
The matter must be transferred
It does not apply and the civil court retains jurisdiction
The Federal Court decides
quiz.why: Clause (1A) only bites where the matter is within Syariah jurisdiction in the first place.

quiz.q: What is the basic structure doctrine, at its narrowest?
options: That all legislation must be proportionate
That the Federal Court may overrule itself
That some fundamental features cannot be removed even by a constitutional amendment
That State law yields to federal law
quiz.why: It is a limit on the power to amend, not a general power of review over ordinary laws.
quiz.source: The Malaysian case law on judicial power and basic structure

quiz.q: Which court decides whether a law is invalid for want of legislative competence?
options: The High Court
The Federal Court, exclusively
The Court of Appeal
Any court seised of the matter
quiz.why: Article 128 gives the Federal Court exclusive jurisdiction over that question.

lessons.title: The general exceptions, and who has to prove them
lessons.summary: Chapter IV of the Penal Code applies to every offence in it. If you want the benefit of an exception you must prove it yourself, and the standard is the balance of probabilities.

sections.keypoint: Chapter IV applies to every offence in the Code, whether or not the section repeats it.

body.text: A man pushes a snatch thief off a motorbike and the thief is badly hurt. Has he committed an offence? The definition of the offence will not tell you. The answer sits in a different part of the Penal Code.

Sections 76 to 106 are called the General Exceptions. They are not defences to particular offences. They apply to every offence in the Code, and to offences under other statutes so far as the Code's general provisions are made applicable.
You will not find any of them mentioned in the section that defines the offence. Section 6 is the reason why.

Every definition of an offence in the Penal Code is to be understood subject to the exceptions in the Chapter entitled 'General Exceptions', though those exceptions are not repeated in the definition itself.
Put simply: every offence in the Code is read with the general exceptions attached, even though the definition never mentions them.
So a homicide answer has looked at only half the picture if it discusses the exceptions to section 300 and never asks about private defence or unsoundness of mind.

sections.keypoint: Mistake, accident, necessity, infancy, unsoundness of mind, intoxication, consent, private defence.

items: **Mistake and being bound to act (ss 76 and 79)** — a person bound by law to do the act. Or a person who, by a mistake of fact and in good faith, believes himself bound or justified by law. Mistake of *fact*, not of law.
**Judicial and official acts (ss 77 and 78)** — a judge acting judicially, and a person acting under a court's judgment or order.
**Accident (s 80)** — an accident or misfortune, without criminal intention or knowledge, while doing a lawful act by lawful means with proper care and caution.
**Necessity (s 81)** — an act likely to cause harm, done without criminal intention and in good faith, to prevent other harm to person or property.
**Infancy (ss 82 and 83)** — nothing done by a child under ten is an offence. Between ten and twelve it turns on whether the child had attained sufficient maturity of understanding.
**Unsoundness of mind (s 84)** — by reason of unsoundness of mind, the person was incapable of knowing the nature of the act. Or incapable of knowing that it was wrong or contrary to law.
**Intoxication (ss 85 and 86)** — narrow. It covers intoxication caused without the person's knowledge or against his will, and intoxication producing insanity.
**Consent (ss 87 to 92)** — with limits set by age and by the degree of harm.
**Private defence (ss 96 to 106)** — of the body, and of property.

sections.keypoint: Private defence has limits: no more harm than necessary, and not where the authorities could be reached.

body.text: Private defence appears in more problems than any other exception. It is a matter of degree, so it is genuinely arguable. Two ideas hold it in place.

Ah Meng is walking home when a man grabs his bag and shoves him. Ah Meng pushes back and the man falls. That is likely to be within the right. Now change one thing. The man drops the bag and walks off, and Ah Meng chases him and hits him with a helmet. The danger was over. That is a different case.
Section 99 sets the outer edges of the right. It says when there is no right at all, and how far the right can ever go.

There is no right of private defence against an act which does not reasonably cause the apprehension of death or grievous hurt, if there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities; and the right in no case extends to inflicting more harm than is necessary.

Put simply: if there was time to go to the authorities and no reasonable fear of death or grievous hurt, there is no right in the first place. And even where the right exists, it never licenses more harm than the situation needs.

Section 100 sets out the cases in which the right of private defence of the body extends to causing death. They include a reasonable apprehension of death, and of grievous hurt, and certain enumerated offences. Section 103 does the same for property.

body.prompt: A man defends himself against an attack, goes further than the danger needed, and kills. He acted in good faith and had no plan. What does the excess do?
options: Nothing — he went too far, so it is murder
It brings the conviction down to culpable homicide not amounting to murder
It leaves the murder conviction and only softens the sentence
body.reveal: Going too far does not simply cancel the defence. Exception 2 to section 300 brings the charge down, so the excess changes the conviction and not only the sentence. If you chose the first answer, you were right that the defence did not stretch that far. The Code just does something else with the excess.

body.text: The commonest error is to treat the right as lost because the response was excessive. Excess goes to whether the right extended *this far*. An accused who exceeds the right, in good faith and without premeditation, may still bring the charge down. Murder becomes culpable homicide not amounting to murder, under Exception 2 to section 300. Those are different convictions and they carry different sentences.

body.title: Section 99 asks whether the right exists at all
body.caption: Excess does not destroy a right that existed. It goes to whether the right extended this far. Answering the two questions in the wrong order is the commonest error in this area.
body.alt: A question — was there a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, or no time to go to the authorities? — branching two ways. No: section 99 means no right arises, and the enquiry ends. Yes: the right exists, and the next question is how far it extends, with section 100 setting out when it reaches causing death.
body.question: Reasonable fear of death or grievous hurt, or no time to reach the authorities?

branches.label: The right exists — now ask how far
branches.note: s 100 lists when it reaches causing death

sections.keypoint: Section 105 puts the burden on the accused, on the balance of probabilities — not on the prosecution.

body.text: The prosecution must prove the offence. But if you want the benefit of an exception, the work of proving it falls on you.

When a person is accused of any offence, the burden of proving the existence of circumstances bringing the case within any of the General Exceptions in the Penal Code is upon him, and the court shall presume the absence of those circumstances.
Put simply: the court starts by assuming the exception does not apply, and it is for the accused to show that it does.
That is a legal burden on the accused, and it is discharged on the balance of probabilities — more likely than not. It is not the criminal standard.
The prosecution's own burden is untouched by any of this. It must still prove the offence beyond reasonable doubt, and it carries that burden throughout.

Rosli is charged after a fight and says he was acting in self-defence. He does not have to make the court sure of it. He has to make the court think it more likely than not. If he does, the exception is his.

Do not write that the accused must merely 'raise' the exception, and that the prosecution must then disprove it beyond reasonable doubt. That is the English position on some defences. It is not what section 105 says.

body.title: Two burdens, at two different standards

items: Must prove every element of the offence.
Beyond reasonable doubt.
This burden is untouched by any exception, and it never shifts.
It carries that burden throughout.
The court starts by assuming the exception does not apply.
A legal burden, on the accused, to show that it does.
On the balance of probabilities — more likely than not.
**Not** merely raising it and leaving the prosecution to disprove it. That is the English position, and it is not ours.

quiz.q: Who has to prove a general exception, and to what standard?
options: On the prosecution, beyond reasonable doubt
On the accused, on the balance of probabilities
On the accused, beyond reasonable doubt
It is a purely evidential burden
quiz.why: Section 105 puts a legal burden on the accused and directs the court to presume the circumstances are absent.

quiz.q: Section 79 of the Penal Code excuses an act done under a mistake of what?
options: Law
Identity only
Fact
Either fact or law
quiz.why: A mistake of fact, made in good faith, believing oneself justified by law. A mistake about the law does not excuse.

quiz.q: Under s 82, a child under what age cannot commit an offence at all?
options: Ten
Seven
Twelve
Fourteen
quiz.why: Nothing done by a child under ten is an offence. Between ten and twelve the question is sufficient maturity of understanding.

quiz.q: An accused goes further than the right of private defence allowed, and kills. What is the likely effect?
options: The right is simply lost and murder stands
It is a complete defence anyway
Murder may be reduced to culpable homicide not amounting to murder
It goes only to sentence
quiz.why: Exception 2 to s 300 covers exceeding the right in good faith and without premeditation.

quiz.q: Under s 99(3), when is there no right of private defence?
options: Whenever the attacker is unarmed
Whenever the police could be called
Whenever the accused struck first
Where there is time to go to the public authorities and no fear of death or grievous hurt
quiz.why: Both halves matter. Time to seek protection is not enough on its own if death or grievous hurt is reasonably feared.

quiz.q: Why does Chapter IV matter to a case about a killing?
options: They apply only to offences against property
The exceptions apply to every offence in the Code, s 300 included
They replace the exceptions to s 300
They apply only in the Sessions Court
quiz.why: Section 6 makes every definition of an offence subject to the general exceptions.

lessons.title: Bail, and the shape of a criminal trial
lessons.summary: Whether bail is available turns on how the offence is classified. The trial then stops twice to ask a question, and the two questions are not the same one.

sections.keypoint: Bailable means as of right; non-bailable means discretionary, not unavailable.

body.text: Someone is arrested on a Friday night. The first thing the family asks is whether he can come home while the case runs. That is bail.
Bail is a promise to come back to court, usually backed by money or by a surety. A surety is a person who agrees to be answerable if the accused does not turn up.

body.prompt: Someone is arrested on a Friday night. The charge is listed in the Code as a **non-bailable** offence. Can he come home before the trial?
options: No — that is what the word means
Yes, if the court decides to allow it
Only once he has been charged in court and has pleaded
body.reveal: He can, if the court is willing. Non-bailable does not mean bail is unavailable. It means bail is in the court's hands rather than the accused's right. The word misleads everybody the first time. Read it as 'bail is not automatic'.

body.text: Whether bail is available depends on how the offence is classified, and the First Schedule to the Criminal Procedure Code does that offence by offence. The vocabulary misleads everybody the first time: 'non-bailable' does not mean bail is unavailable.

items: **Bailable offence** — the accused is entitled to be released on bail. It is not a discretion.
**Non-bailable offence** — bail is in the discretion of the court, subject to the restrictions in s 388.

**Offences punishable with death or imprisonment for life** — the general position under s 388(1) is that a person shall not be released on bail. The section then has provisos, which include provision for young persons, women, and the sick or infirm.

body.text: A person accused of a bailable offence shall be released on bail; a person accused of a non-bailable offence may be released on bail, in the discretion of the court.
Put simply: bailable means the court must grant bail. Non-bailable means the court may.
Some statutes outside the Code create their own bail regimes, and some exclude bail altogether. Always check the statute creating the offence before applying the Code's scheme.

body.caption: What the classification decides
rows: As of right — the accused shall be released
In the court's discretion under s 388 — *not* unavailable
Punishable with death or life imprisonment
Restricted by s 388(1), subject to its provisos
body.note: Special legislation, particularly on security and drugs, often displaces this scheme entirely. Check the statute creating the offence before applying the Code.
body.source: Criminal Procedure Code ss 387, 388 and the First Schedule

sections.keypoint: Where bail is discretionary the real question is whether he will come back, and what happens meanwhile.
sections.h: How the court uses its discretion

body.text: Where bail is discretionary, the court is really asking one thing. Will this person come back to court, and what happens meanwhile if he is out?

The matters weighed are practical ones: whether the accused will run, whether he may interfere with witnesses, how grave the offence is and what sentence it carries. The court also weighs his antecedents, his ties to the place, and the state of the investigation.

Conditions are how those risks are managed — sureties, surrender of a passport, reporting to a police station. Proposing conditions is usually a stronger argument than an assertion that the risk is low.

Encik Zul has run a stall in Ipoh for twenty years and his children are at school there. He is charged with a non-bailable offence. Two local sureties, his passport held by the court, and reporting every Monday answer most of what the court is worried about.

sections.keypoint: Grounds, a lawyer, and a Magistrate within twenty-four hours — the constitutional floor on arrest.

body.text: The Constitution puts a clock on police custody, and it is a short one.

A person arrested shall be informed as soon as may be of the grounds of his arrest and shall be allowed to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of his choice; and shall not be detained beyond twenty-four hours without the authority of a Magistrate.
body.source: Federal Constitution Art 5(3) and 5(4), reflected in the Criminal Procedure Code

body.text: Put simply: you must be told why you were arrested, you may see a lawyer, and after twenty-four hours only a Magistrate can authorise keeping you.

To hold someone longer the police must go to a Magistrate for a remand order under section 117 of the Code. Remand is detention authorised for the purpose of investigation, for the period the Magistrate thinks fit.
That hearing is a real hearing and not a formality. The police must show why further detention is needed.
Check the current maximum remand periods in section 117. They are graduated by the length of the sentence the offence carries, and they have been amended.

sections.keypoint: Prima facie case at the close of the prosecution; beyond reasonable doubt at the close of the defence.
sections.h: The two decision points at trial

body.text: A criminal trial stops twice and asks a question. The two questions are different, and merging them is the classic error.
The first stop comes when the prosecution has finished calling its evidence.

At the close of the case for the prosecution the court shall consider whether the prosecution has made out a prima facie case; if it has, the court shall call upon the accused to enter his defence, and if it has not, the court shall record an order of acquittal.
Put simply: at the halfway point the court asks whether the prosecution's evidence, standing alone, would be enough to convict. If it would not, the case ends there and then.
A prima facie case is made out where the evidence, if unrebutted, would warrant a conviction. Prima facie means 'on the face of it' — enough unless it is answered.

That standard has been amended and much discussed. The phrase 'maximum evaluation' comes from that discussion. It means the court must properly evaluate the prosecution evidence at this stage, rather than merely ask whether some evidence exists.

At the close of the defence the question is different and simpler. On the whole of the evidence, has the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt? A defence that raises a reasonable doubt is enough, and it does not have to be believed.

Two witnesses say they saw Kumar near the shop. Kumar says he was elsewhere and calls his sister to say so. The court need not believe the sister. If her evidence leaves the court unsure, that is enough for Kumar.

body.q: At the close of the defence, what does the accused have to do?
options: Prove his account, on the balance of probabilities
Nothing — the prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt
Show a prima facie case of his own
body.why: On the whole of the evidence, the question is whether the prosecution has proved its case. A defence that leaves the court unsure is enough, and it does not have to be believed. The first answer merges the two stages. That burden appears only where a statute puts it on him.

body.text: Do not merge the two stages. Writing that the accused must *prove* his defence at the second stage is wrong. The exception is where a statute places a burden on him, as s 105 of the Evidence Act does for the general exceptions.

body.title: The two decision points ask different questions

left.h: Close of the prosecution case — s 180
items: Has a *prima facie* case been made out?
Evidence which, if unrebutted, would warrant a conviction.
The court evaluates the prosecution evidence properly rather than asking whether any evidence exists.
If not made out: acquittal.
Has the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt on the whole of the evidence?
The defence need only raise a reasonable doubt.
It does not have to be believed.
The burden has not shifted, save where a statute shifts it.

sections.keypoint: Article 145(3) puts prosecutions in the hands of the Public Prosecutor, not the complainant.

body.text: The Public Prosecutor has control and direction of all criminal prosecutions. That is Article 145(3) of the Federal Constitution.
A charge can end in two very different ways. An acquittal is final. A discharge not amounting to an acquittal is not: the prosecution remains able to recharge on the same facts.
Say that plainly to a client. People hear the word 'discharged' and go home understanding 'finished'.

quiz.q: What does 'non-bailable offence' mean?
options: Bail cannot be granted
Bail requires the Public Prosecutor's consent
Bail is granted only on appeal
Bail is in the court's discretion
quiz.why: The label misleads. Section 388 makes bail discretionary for these offences, subject to the restrictions in it.

quiz.q: Where is an offence classified as bailable or non-bailable?
options: The Penal Code definition
The charge sheet
The First Schedule to the Criminal Procedure Code
The Courts of Judicature Act 1964
quiz.why: In the First Schedule to the Code, offence by offence. The Penal Code definition does not say.

quiz.q: How long may a person be held after arrest without a Magistrate's authority?
options: Forty-eight hours
Seven days
Until investigations conclude
Twenty-four hours
quiz.why: Art 5(4) sets twenty-four hours. Anything longer needs a remand order under s 117 of the Code.

quiz.q: What is the question at the close of the prosecution case?
options: Whether a prima facie case has been made out
Whether guilt is proved beyond reasonable doubt
Whether the accused has a defence
Whether the charge is properly framed
quiz.why: Section 180 asks whether a prima facie case is made out. If it is, the accused is called to enter his defence.

quiz.q: At the close of the defence, what must the accused's evidence achieve?
options: Prove innocence on the balance of probabilities
Be believed by the court
Prove innocence beyond reasonable doubt
Raise a reasonable doubt
quiz.why: The prosecution's burden never shifts, save where a statute shifts it. The defence need not be believed.
quiz.source: Standard criminal standard of proof; the prosecution's burden does not shift save where a statute shifts it

quiz.q: What is the effect of a discharge not amounting to an acquittal?
options: The prosecution is at an end
It bars any further proceedings
It is the same as an acquittal
The accused may be recharged on the same facts
quiz.why: It is not a final determination, which is exactly why the difference has to be explained to a client.
quiz.source: Criminal Procedure Code; a discharge not amounting to an acquittal is not a final determination

lessons.title: When an agreement can be undone: the vitiating factors
lessons.summary: Free consent is defined by the five things that spoil it. Each has its own section in the Contracts Act 1950, and they do not all have the same consequence.

sections.keypoint: A contract needs free consent, and section 14 defines that by what removes it.

body.text: Puan Aini signs a paper agreeing to sell her land for RM30,000. She signs because the buyer told her the land floods every year and is worth nothing. It does not flood. She agreed, but she did not agree with her eyes open.
The law has a list of the things that spoil consent. It is a closed list, and it is in the Contracts Act 1950. Start with what a contract needs in the first place.
An agreement is a contract if it is made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and is not expressly declared to be void.
Put simply: four things are needed. Consent that is free, parties old enough and of sound mind, a lawful price and a lawful purpose, and no provision declaring the agreement void.
Consideration is the price of a promise — what each side gives in exchange for what it gets. That leaves the phrase in the middle, free consent, which the next section defines.
Consent is said to be free when it is not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, or mistake.
Put simply: consent is free unless one of five named things caused it. Lawyers call those five the **vitiating factors**, from a word that means to spoil or impair.

Section 14 is a closed list, and ss 15 to 23 supply the statutory definitions. An answer that reasons from English duress, or from English misrepresentation, has started in the wrong place. It usually gets the consequence wrong as well.

sections.keypoint: Coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, mistake — each with a statutory definition narrower than the everyday word.

items: **Coercion (s 15)** — committing or threatening to commit an act forbidden by the Penal Code. Or unlawfully detaining property, or threatening to detain it, to the prejudice of any person. It must be done with the intention of causing a person to enter into the agreement. Notice how much narrower that is than 'pressure'.

**Undue influence (s 16)** — the relations between the parties are such that one can dominate the will of the other, and he uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage. Section 16(2) gives instances of such a position. Where the transaction appears unconscionable, s 16(3) puts it on the dominant party to show the contract was not induced by undue influence.

**Fraud (s 17)** — suggesting a fact is true when you do not believe it to be true. Also active concealment, and a promise made with no intention of performing it. Mere silence is not fraud, unless there is a duty to speak, or the silence is in itself equivalent to speech.

**Misrepresentation (s 18)** — a positive assertion, not warranted by the information the maker has, of something untrue that he believes to be true. It also covers certain breaches of duty, and causing a party to make a mistake about the subject matter. The difference from fraud is honesty.
**Mistake (ss 21 to 23)** — a mistake by both parties as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement makes it void. A mistake as to a law in force in Malaysia does not.

body.text: Pak Hamid is eighty and unwell. His nephew handles his bank account, his papers and his medicine. The nephew has him sign a transfer of the house for RM1. The relationship is the point: the nephew was in a position to dominate his uncle's will, and the transaction appears unconscionable. Section 16(3) then puts it on the nephew to show the transfer was not induced by undue influence.
Unconscionable is not the same as unwise. People are entitled to make bad bargains, and the courts do not rewrite them. The word points at a transaction so one-sided that it calls for an explanation.

sections.keypoint: Coercion, fraud and misrepresentation make an agreement voidable; a shared mistake of essential fact makes it void.

body.text: Two words do a great deal of work here and they are easy to confuse.
**Void** means the agreement had no legal effect from the beginning. There is nothing there to keep. **Voidable** means the agreement is valid and binding until the innocent party elects to undo it.
Which one you get depends on which vitiating factor you are dealing with.

body.prompt: Aini signed because the buyer told her the land floods. It does not flood. Is there a contract at all?
options: No — a lie wipes the agreement out from the start
Yes, and it binds her until she chooses to undo it
Yes, and the only thing she can ask for is money
body.reveal: There is a contract. Coercion, fraud and misrepresentation make an agreement voidable rather than void, so it stands until the wronged party takes it down. If you picked the first answer, that instinct is not wasted. It is right about a mistake made by both parties, which section 21 does make void.

body.text: When consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused.
Put simply: coercion, fraud and misrepresentation give the wronged party a choice. The contract stands unless and until that party takes it down.

She may rescind it — unwind it and put both sides back where they started. Or she may insist that the contract be performed, and that she be put in the position she would have been in if what she was told had been true.
The right to rescind can be lost. It goes if she affirms the contract after learning the truth, if she waits too long, or if restitution has become impossible.
A mistake by both parties about an essential fact is a different case. Section 21 makes that agreement void. There is no election to make, because there is nothing to affirm.

Section 66 then deals with restoration. A person who has received an advantage under an agreement discovered to be void must restore it, or make compensation for it. The same goes for a contract that becomes void. It does the work an English lawyer would look for in restitution.

Aini learns that the flood story was false. She may rescind, hand back the price and take her land. Or she may hold the buyer to the sale on the footing that what he said was true. What she may not do is wait two years, spend the money, and then rescind.

body.title: Which factor you have decides which word you get
body.caption: The practical difference is the election. Voidable leaves the choice with the wronged party; void leaves nobody anything to elect about.
body.alt: A question — which vitiating factor caused the consent? — branching two ways. Coercion, fraud or misrepresentation under section 19: the agreement is voidable, and the wronged party may rescind or may affirm and insist on performance. A mistake by both parties as to an essential fact falls under section 21. That agreement is void from the start. There is no election to make, and section 66 handles restoration.
body.question: Which factor caused the consent?

branches.label: Voidable (s 19)
branches.note: she elects: rescind, or affirm and be put in the true position

sections.keypoint: Capacity under s 11, and an unlawful object or consideration under s 24, are separate ways to fail.

body.text: Two more requirements sit alongside free consent, and both come from section 10.

Section 11 makes a person competent to contract if he is of the age of majority, of sound mind, and not disqualified from contracting by any law. The age of majority is eighteen, under the Age of Majority Act 1971.
What happens to a minor's agreement in Malaysia is governed by our own statutes and our own authorities. Do not assume the English infancy rules. Check current Malaysian authority instead.
The other requirement is that what the parties are doing must be lawful. Section 24 says when it is not.

The consideration or object of an agreement is unlawful if it is forbidden by law, or would defeat any law, or is fraudulent, or involves injury to person or property, or the court regards it as immoral or opposed to public policy; every agreement of which the object or consideration is unlawful is void.
Put simply: if the purpose or the price of the deal falls into any of those categories, the whole agreement is void.
Two people agree that one will pay the other RM5,000 to withdraw a police report. Whatever they wrote down, that is not a contract any court will enforce. Section 24 makes it void.

Do not reach for 'illegality' as one big general doctrine. Section 24 lists the categories, and s 25 deals with an agreement that is only partly unlawful. The argument in a real case is about which limb of s 24 is engaged.

sections.keypoint: Name the factor and its section, state the definition, apply it both ways, then say void or voidable.

body.text: Name the vitiating factor and its section. State the statutory definition. Apply it to the facts, and argue it both ways where it is arguable.
Then state the consequence — void or voidable — and what follows from that for the remedy your client actually wants. Answers lose their footing in that last step far more often than the first.

items.h: Name the factor, and its section.
items.text: Coercion is s 15, undue influence s 16, fraud s 17, misrepresentation s 18, mistake ss 21 to 23. The section number is part of the answer.
Quote the Act, not an English formulation of the same idea. The definitions here are statutory and they do not match the English doctrines.
Argue it both ways wherever it is genuinely arguable. Most of the marks live in this step.
Void, or voidable. This follows from which factor you named, not from how serious the conduct feels.

items.h: Say what follows for the remedy.
items.text: Rescission, affirmation with compensation, or restoration under s 66. Answers lose their footing when they stop at the label.

quiz.q: Both parties are mistaken about a fact essential to their agreement. What is the effect?
options: The agreement is voidable
The agreement is void
The agreement is valid
The agreement is unenforceable but not void
quiz.why: Section 21 makes it void, so there is nothing to affirm. Voidability under s 19 belongs to coercion, fraud and misrepresentation.

quiz.q: Which section defines coercion, and what does it require?
options: Section 17 — a false suggestion of fact
Section 16 — domination of the will
Section 14 — any improper pressure
Section 15 — an act forbidden by the Penal Code, or unlawful detention of property
quiz.why: The statutory definition is far narrower than 'pressure', and that is where English duress reasoning goes wrong here.

quiz.q: When does staying silent amount to fraud under s 17?
options: Always, if a material fact is withheld
Where there is a duty to speak, or the silence is equivalent to speech
Never
Only in contracts of insurance
quiz.why: The explanation to s 17 sets out both limbs. Silence on its own is not fraud.

quiz.q: What separates misrepresentation under s 18 from fraud under s 17?
options: The statement is about the future
The maker believes what he says is true
It concerns a third party
It is made in writing
quiz.why: Section 18 covers an assertion not warranted by the information the maker has, though he believes it true.

quiz.q: Someone has received a benefit under an agreement discovered to be void. Which section makes him give it back?
options: Section 66
Section 24
Section 19
Section 74
quiz.why: Section 66 does the work that restitution does in other systems.

quiz.q: What is the age of majority for capacity to contract?
options: Twenty-one
Sixteen
Eighteen
Depends on the State
quiz.why: Eighteen, under the Age of Majority Act 1971, read with s 11 of the Contracts Act 1950.
quiz.source: Age of Majority Act 1971; Contracts Act 1950 s 11

lessons.title: Breach, damages, and the trouble with an agreed sum
lessons.summary: Section 74 measures the compensation. Section 75 governs a sum the parties named in advance, and the law on that has moved in Malaysia within the last decade.

sections.keypoint: Section 40 lets the innocent party end the contract — but that right is an election and can be lost.

body.text: Encik Lim pays a RM5,000 deposit for a second-hand van. A week before delivery the seller says he has sold it to somebody else. What can Lim do?
He has two paths open and he has to pick one. He can treat the contract as over and claim what the breach cost him. Or he can hold the seller to it and keep pressing for the van.

When a party to a contract has refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing, his promise in its entirety, the promisee may put an end to the contract, unless he has signified by words or conduct his acquiescence in its continuance.
Put simply: if the other side refuses to perform at all, you may call the contract off. You lose that right if you have shown that you want the contract to carry on.
The promisee is the person the promise was made to. Ending the contract is an election — a choice, made once, and capable of being lost.
A party who keeps pressing for performance after a repudiation may be held to have affirmed the contract. Affirmation leaves him with damages only.
Time is dealt with by ss 56 and 57. Whether time is of the essence is a question of the parties' intention. A stipulation as to time in a sale of goods or of land is not automatically essential.

sections.keypoint: Section 74 is the rule in Hadley v Baxendale, enacted: loss arising naturally, or within contemplation.

body.text: Damages are meant to put the injured party where performance would have put him. Not better off, and not worse off. Section 74 is where that measure comes from.

When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by the breach is entitled to receive compensation for any loss or damage caused to him which naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach. Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage.

Put simply: you can recover the loss that would ordinarily follow from such a breach. You can also recover unusual loss, but only if the other side knew about the risk when the contract was made. Loss that is remote is not recoverable at all.

Those two limbs will look familiar. This is the rule in *Hadley v Baxendale* (1854) 9 Exch 341, an English Exchequer decision, put into statute. That matters for how you argue it: the starting point is the statutory words, with the English cases as illustration rather than as the source of the rule.

Lim wanted the van for deliveries. Hiring a replacement costs him RM100 a day, and that is ordinary loss under the first limb. Now suppose that when they struck the deal he told the seller he needed the van for one large job worth RM40,000. That loss may fall under the second limb, because the seller knew of it.

The explanation to section 74 adds a practical point. In estimating the loss, the means available for remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance must be taken into account. That is the statutory foothold for mitigation.
Mitigation is the duty to take reasonable steps to limit your own loss. If a similar van could be hired down the road, Lim cannot sit still for three months and send the seller the bill.

body.q: Lim never mentioned the RM40,000 job when the deal was struck. Can he recover that loss?
options: Yes — it followed from the breach
No — unusual loss counts only if the seller knew of the risk when the contract was made
Yes, if he tells the seller as soon as the van fails to arrive
body.why: The second limb of section 74 turns on what the parties knew when they made the contract. It does not turn on what the seller learns afterwards. The trap is timing. The everyday cost of hiring a replacement is still recoverable under the first limb.

sections.keypoint: Section 75 governs a sum named in the contract, and what counts as reasonable moved with Cubic Electronics.
sections.h: A sum named in the contract

body.text: Many contracts name a figure in advance. 'If you are late, you pay RM500 for every day.' Is that figure simply payable when the day comes?

body.prompt: The contract says RM500 for every day the van is late. It arrives six days late. Is the seller simply liable for RM3,000?
options: Yes — both sides agreed that figure in advance
Only reasonable compensation, and never more than RM3,000
Nothing, because a fixed sum like that is a penalty
body.reveal: The named figure is a ceiling, not a bill. Section 75 gives reasonable compensation up to the sum named, so what Lim actually recovers still has to be justified. If you picked the first answer, you read the clause the way the parties wrote it, and in some countries that is what you would get.

body.text: When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, the party complaining of the breach is entitled to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named.
Put simply: the named figure is a ceiling, not an automatic entitlement. What is actually paid is reasonable compensation, up to that figure.

A plaintiff is the person who brings the case. For a long period the Malaysian position on what a plaintiff had to show came from *Selva Kumar a/l Murugiah v Thiagarajah a/l Retnasamy* [1995] 1 MLJ 817 (FC).
He had to prove actual loss, and he recovered only what he proved, subject to the named sum as a ceiling. The named sum was in effect a cap and nothing more.

That was revisited in *Cubic Electronics Sdn Bhd (in liquidation) v Mars Telecommunications Sdn Bhd* [2019] 2 CLJ 723 (FC). The Federal Court reformulated the approach, drawing on the UK Supreme Court decision in *Cavendish Square Holding BV v Talal El Makdessi* [2015] UKSC 67.
Attention now goes to two questions. Does the clause protect a legitimate interest? And is the sum out of all proportion to that interest?

This is the single most important 'check before you rely on it' point in the contract module. State the sequence, name both cases, and check whether anything has been decided since. An answer that gives only *Selva Kumar* is out of date, and one that gives only *Cubic Electronics* has not shown it understands what changed.

body.title: Section 75 has moved once, and could again
body.caption: An answer giving only one of these two has not shown that it knows the position changed. Check whether anything has been decided since.
body.alt: Three points. In 1950 the Contracts Act enacted section 75: reasonable compensation, not exceeding the sum named. In 1995 Selva Kumar held that a plaintiff must prove actual loss, with the named sum as a ceiling. In 2019 Cubic Electronics reformulated the approach around legitimate interest and proportionality to it.

events.label: Contracts Act 1950, s 75 enacted
events.note: reasonable compensation, not exceeding the sum named

events.label: Selva Kumar v Thiagarajah (FC)
events.note: a plaintiff must prove actual loss; the named sum is a ceiling

events.label: Cubic Electronics v Mars (FC)
events.note: reformulated: legitimate interest, and proportionality to it

sections.keypoint: Where damages cannot do the job, the Specific Relief Act 1950 governs — not the Contracts Act.

body.text: Some things money cannot replace. A particular piece of land is the standard example, because no two lots are the same.

Damages are the primary remedy. Specific performance — an order compelling actual performance rather than damages — is discretionary, and it comes from a separate statute, the Specific Relief Act 1950.

Section 11 of that Act sets out the cases in which specific performance may be granted. Section 20 sets out those in which it cannot. Two common refusals are where compensation in money is adequate relief, and where the contract would require continuous supervision.
A buyer of a house in Cheras can usually ask the court to order the sale through. A buyer of a hundred bags of cement usually cannot. He can buy cement elsewhere and claim the difference in price.

The Specific Relief Act is a separate statute with its own scheme. Do not answer a specific performance question out of the Contracts Act, and do not import English equitable discretion in place of the Act's sections.

sections.keypoint: Contract, breach, termination or affirmation, measure — and only then any agreed sum.

body.text: Establish the contract, then the breach, then whether the innocent party terminated or affirmed, then the measure of loss.
Only then reach any agreed sum. Answers that start with the liquidated damages clause tend to skip the question whether there is a recoverable loss at all.

quiz.q: Section 74 of the Contracts Act 1950 puts which familiar rule into statute?
options: The rule in Hong Kong Fir
The rule in Pinnel's Case
The rule in Carlill
The rule in Hadley v Baxendale
quiz.why: The two limbs — loss arising naturally, and loss within the parties' contemplation — are the statutory form of it.

quiz.q: Which case reformulated the Malaysian approach to a sum named in the contract under s 75?
options: Selva Kumar v Thiagarajah
Kepong Prospecting v Schmidt
Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San
Cubic Electronics v Mars Telecommunications
quiz.why: The Federal Court there moved away from the strict requirement of proving actual loss, drawing on Cavendish v Makdessi.
quiz.source: Cubic Electronics Sdn Bhd (in liquidation) v Mars Telecommunications Sdn Bhd [2019] 2 CLJ 723 (FC); Cavendish Square Holding BV v Talal El Makdessi [2015] UKSC 67

quiz.q: Under s 40, what may a promisee do when the other side refuses to perform at all?
options: Claim the named sum automatically
Seek specific performance only
Put an end to the contract, unless he has acquiesced in its continuance
Nothing until the time for performance passes
quiz.why: Ending the contract is an election, and it can be lost by affirming the contract instead.

quiz.q: Which statute governs specific performance in Malaysia?
options: The Contracts Act 1950
The Civil Law Act 1956
The Specific Relief Act 1950
The Rules of Court 2012
quiz.why: The Specific Relief Act 1950 has its own scheme, in ss 11 and 20 among others. Do not answer out of the Contracts Act.

quiz.q: Why is specific performance a live remedy in a sale of land?
options: Land contracts are always in writing
The National Land Code requires it
Damages are treated as inadequate for land
Injunctions are unavailable
quiz.why: Whether damages are adequate is the gateway question under the Act, and for land they are treated as inadequate.

quiz.q: What is the right order of analysis in a remedies question?
options: Contract, breach, termination or affirmation, measure, then any agreed sum
Specific performance first
Agreed sum first, then loss
Loss first, then contract
quiz.why: Starting at the clause skips the question whether there is a recoverable loss at all.
quiz.source: Standard analytical order for a contract remedies question
