lessons.title: Causation, remoteness, and the injured person's own fault
lessons.summary: Duty and breach take you halfway. Causation, remoteness and apportionment under s 12 of the Civil Law Act 1956 are where negligence claims are actually won and lost.

sections.keypoint: But for the breach, would the damage have happened? If it would, the claim fails there.
sections.h: Did the carelessness cause the harm?

body.text: Proving that somebody was careless is not enough. You must also show that the carelessness made a difference to what happened.
The plaintiff is the person bringing the claim. The defendant is the person being sued.
The plaintiff must show that, but for the defendant's breach, the damage would not have occurred.
body.source: Standard common law test of factual causation; applied in Malaysia

body.text: Put simply: take the carelessness out of the story and run it again. If the harm still happens, the carelessness did not cause it.

A man goes to a hospital casualty department after swallowing poison. The officer on duty sends him away without examining him. He dies that night. If he would have died even with treatment, the negligence caused no loss. The claim fails on causation however plain the breach was.

The test breaks down in two familiar situations. One is multiple sufficient causes, where each alone would have caused the damage. The other is scientific uncertainty about which of several exposures caused the injury.
Both have generated exceptional approaches. Identify them as exceptions. Do not use them as the general rule.

sections.keypoint: A later act may break the chain — a deliberate third-party one usually does, a foreseeable one usually does not.

body.text: A careless driver leaves Siti with a broken leg. On the way to hospital a second driver crashes into the ambulance. Who answers for what?
A later act may break the chain. A deliberate wrongful act by a third party usually does. An act that was foreseeable, or one the defendant's own negligence made likely, usually does not.
The plaintiff's own unreasonable conduct can break the chain too. Lawyers call an intervening act that breaks it a *novus actus interveniens*.
Do not use *novus actus* and contributory negligence interchangeably. The first defeats the claim. The second reduces it. Choosing the wrong one is a substantive error dressed as a vocabulary slip.

sections.keypoint: The kind of damage must be foreseeable; the extent need not, which is where the eggshell skull sits.
sections.h: The kind of harm, not how bad

body.text: Suppose the harm was caused, and nothing broke the chain. There is still a limit on how far liability reaches.

body.prompt: Ahmad is knocked off his motorcycle and takes a modest knock to the head. Because of a rare condition nobody knew of, he can never work again. What does the careless driver pay for?
options: The ordinary head injury only — nobody could foresee the rest
All of it
Nothing, because it was the condition and not the crash that ruined him
body.reveal: All of it. Foreseeability is about the *kind* of harm, not about how bad it turns out. A knock to the head is foreseeable from a road accident, and the driver gets no discount for finding a fragile victim. The first answer is the fair-minded one. It is also the one the law sets aside.

body.text: A defendant is liable only for damage of a kind that was reasonably foreseeable. Where the kind of damage is foreseeable, it is no answer that its extent was not.
body.source: The Wagon Mound (No 1); applied in the Malaysian courts

body.text: Put simply: ask whether harm of that *sort* was foreseeable. If it was, the defendant does not escape because it turned out worse than anyone expected.

A workshop leaves a hot pipe uncovered and a worker is burned. Burns are a foreseeable kind of harm from an uncovered hot pipe. The workshop does not escape because the burn turned out far worse than expected.

The 'eggshell skull' principle sits inside this. A defendant takes the victim as found. Foreseeability governs the type of injury; the plaintiff's particular susceptibility governs how bad it turns out to be, and it does not reduce the claim.
Ahmad is knocked off his motorcycle and takes a modest blow to the head. Because of a rare condition he already had, it leaves him unable to work. The driver pays for all of it.

sections.keypoint: Section 12 of the Civil Law Act 1956 apportions rather than defeats — reason to a proportion, do not assert one.
sections.h: When the victim was partly to blame

body.text: A motorcyclist wearing no helmet is knocked down by a car that ran a red light. The car is plainly at fault. But the head injury would have been much less serious with a helmet.
Once, that was fatal to the whole claim. Contributory negligence used to be a complete defence, and the injured person walked away with nothing. One section changed that.

Where any person suffers damage as the result partly of his own fault and partly of the fault of any other person, a claim shall not be defeated by reason of the fault of the person suffering the damage, but the damages recoverable shall be reduced to such extent as the court thinks just and equitable having regard to the claimant's share in the responsibility for the damage.
Put simply: your own carelessness no longer destroys your claim. It cuts the award by whatever share of the blame is yours.
So the question is now a proportion. A good answer proposes a figure and gives reasons for it, rather than asserting only that damages 'will be reduced'.

Where somebody has died, the same Act governs the claims that follow. There is a claim for the dependants and a claim for the estate. The heads of damage recoverable are constrained by the Act rather than left at large.

Damages for death and personal injury in Malaysia are shaped by statute in ways that differ from English practice. Check the current text of the Civil Law Act 1956 before stating what is recoverable and how it is calculated.

body.title: Two doctrines that are constantly confused

items: A later act breaks the chain of causation.
The defendant is not liable for what follows it.
**Defeats** the claim.
A deliberate third-party act usually breaks it; a foreseeable one usually does not.
The claimant failed to take reasonable care for their own safety.
Section 12, Civil Law Act 1956.
**Reduces** the damages, by a proportion the court finds just and equitable.
Before that section it was a complete defence — older material must be read with care.

sections.keypoint: Duty, breach, factual causation, legal causation, remoteness, damage — then defences.

body.text: Take the elements in order and do not skip forward. Duty, breach, factual causation, legal causation, remoteness, damage. Defences and apportionment come last.
The order is not stylistic. Each step assumes the one before it, and an answer that argues remoteness before establishing breach is arguing about nothing.

quiz.q: A doctor negligently sends away a patient who would have died anyway. What defeats the claim?
options: Remoteness
Absence of duty
Factual causation — the but-for test
Contributory negligence
quiz.why: The breach caused no loss, so the claim fails at causation however clear the breach was.
quiz.source: Standard common law on factual causation; the but-for test

quiz.q: What is the effect of contributory negligence in Malaysia?
options: The claim is defeated entirely
Damages are apportioned under s 12 of the Civil Law Act 1956
It goes only to costs
It breaks the chain of causation
quiz.why: Section 12 replaced the old complete defence with an apportionment of the damages.

quiz.q: Which is the correct statement of the remoteness rule?
options: The kind of damage must be foreseeable; the extent need not be
Both the kind and the extent must be foreseeable
Neither need be foreseeable once breach is proved
Only economic loss must be foreseeable
quiz.why: That is the Wagon Mound test, with the eggshell skull principle sitting inside it.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a novus actus interveniens and contributory negligence?
options: They are the same thing
The first applies only to third parties, the second only to defendants
The first is statutory, the second is common law
The first defeats the claim; the second reduces it
quiz.why: The first defeats the claim and the second reduces it. Using them interchangeably is a substantive error.
quiz.source: Civil Law Act 1956 s 12; standard common law on intervening acts

quiz.q: In what order should a negligence answer proceed?
options: Damage, duty, breach, causation
Breach, duty, defences, causation
Causation, duty, breach, remoteness
Duty, breach, causation, remoteness, damage, defences
quiz.why: Each step assumes the one before it. Arguing remoteness before breach is arguing about nothing.
quiz.source: Standard classification; the elements of the tort of negligence

reading.where: the chapters on causation, remoteness and defences

lessons.source: Civil Law Act 1956 s 12; The Wagon Mound (No 1) [1961] AC 388 as applied in Malaysia; standard common law on factual and legal causation.
lessons.verify: Check s 12 and the death-and-personal-injury provisions of the Civil Law Act 1956 against the current text, and check the current Malaysian authority on the duty of care test before assuming any particular English formulation applies here.
lessons.plateCaption: The chain of causation, and the link a grossly negligent later act may break. Breaking it defeats the claim; contributing to it only reduces.

lessons.title: Defamation: the three elements, and the defences that matter
lessons.summary: Defamatory meaning, reference to the plaintiff, and publication. The Defamation Act 1957 then governs the defences, and the line between libel and slander still does work.

sections.keypoint: A false message in a group of forty neighbours: what exactly must be proved?

body.text: A WhatsApp group of forty neighbours gets a message. 'Careful with Puan Nora — she takes money from the surau fund.' It is not true. What must Nora show before she can sue?

items: **The words are defamatory.** They tend to lower her in the estimation of right-thinking members of society generally. Or they expose her to hatred, ridicule or contempt, or cause her to be shunned or avoided.
**The words refer to her.** Naming her is not necessary. It is enough that reasonable readers, knowing the surrounding circumstances, would understand the words as referring to her.
**The words were published.** Published here means communicated to at least one person other than her. Forty neighbours is thirty-nine more than she needs.

body.text: All three must be established before any defence is reached. An answer that opens with qualified privilege has assumed the case it ought to be proving.

body.title: The order the questions come in
body.caption: All three elements come before any defence. An answer that opens with qualified privilege has assumed the case it was supposed to prove.
body.alt: Five stages in order. The words are defamatory. They refer to the plaintiff. They were published to at least one other person. Only then are the defences reached. Malice comes last, and only against qualified privilege and fair comment.

steps.label: Defamatory
steps.note: tends to lower her in others' estimation

steps.label: Published
steps.note: to at least one person other than her

steps.label: Then malice
steps.note: only against qualified privilege and fair comment

sections.keypoint: Libel is permanent, slander transient — and slander usually needs special damage, subject to statutory exceptions.

body.text: Libel is defamation in permanent form — writing, print, a posted picture. Slander is defamation in transient form, such as something said out loud.
The distinction still matters. Slander is generally actionable only on proof of special damage, meaning some actual measurable loss. Libel needs no such proof.
The Defamation Act 1957 preserves the categories and modifies them. Two kinds of spoken words are singled out.

Words spoken and published which impute unchastity or adultery to any woman or girl, and words calculated to disparage a person in any office, profession, calling, trade or business held or carried on by him at the time of publication, do not require proof of special damage.
Put simply: for those two kinds of spoken words, the plaintiff does not have to show she lost anything. The words are actionable on their own.

A supplier tells three shopkeepers that Encik Faizal, a plumber, does shoddy work and overcharges. Those are spoken words calculated to disparage him in his trade. He does not have to prove he lost a particular job.

Publication online has made the permanent-or-transient line harder to apply than it sounds. Check the current Malaysian authority on how internet publication is classified before assuming it is libel.

body.title: Permanent or transient, and what follows
body.caption: The line is harder to draw online than it sounds, and the current Malaysian authority on internet publication is worth checking rather than assuming.
body.alt: A question — is the form permanent or transient? — branching two ways. Permanent, such as writing or a posted picture: libel, actionable without proof of loss. Transient, such as spoken words: slander. That generally needs special damage. The exception is words imputing unchastity to a woman, or disparaging a person in their office, profession, calling or trade.
body.question: Permanent form, or transient?

branches.label: Slander
branches.note: needs special damage, unless within the Act's two categories

sections.keypoint: Justification, fair comment, absolute and qualified privilege, apology and offer of amends.

body.text: Words can be defamatory and still not actionable. The Act and the common law give a publisher several answers.

items: **Justification** — the imputation is true in substance and in fact. Truth is a complete answer. Under s 8 the defence does not fail merely because the truth of every charge is not proved. That is so where the remaining charges do not materially injure the plaintiff's reputation, given the truth of the rest.
**Fair comment** — an honest comment, on a matter of public interest, based on facts truly stated. Section 9 addresses the position where not every allegation of fact is proved true.
**Absolute privilege** — statements in Parliament and in judicial proceedings, which no malice defeats.
**Qualified privilege** — an occasion where the maker has a duty or interest in making the statement, and the recipient a corresponding interest in receiving it. Defeated by malice.
**Apology and payment into court**, under the Act's own provisions, which have procedural conditions attached.
**Offer of amends**, again on the statute's terms.

body.text: A former employer is asked for a reference and says honestly that the worker was often absent. The employer has an interest in answering, and the new employer an interest in knowing. That is a privileged occasion — unless the former employer was acting out of spite.

Whether, and how far, the *Reynolds* line of responsible-journalism privilege forms part of Malaysian law has been argued in our courts, and should not be assumed either way. If your answer needs it, cite a Malaysian decision.

sections.keypoint: Malice is not an element; it defeats qualified privilege and fair comment.

body.prompt: The neighbour who sent that message about Puan Nora plainly cannot stand her. Does she have to prove he meant her harm?
options: Yes — the tort is about attacking a reputation on purpose
No — she never has to prove ill will
Only if the words were spoken rather than written
body.reveal: She does not. She proves the three things in the first section and stops. Ill will feels like the heart of it. It is usually why people end up in court. But it is not part of what she must show, and where it does its work is set out below.

body.text: Malice is not an element of the tort. A plaintiff does not have to prove that the publisher was hostile.
It matters in exactly two places. It defeats qualified privilege, and it defeats fair comment. Establishing that a publisher disliked the plaintiff does not by itself establish liability.

Damages are at large, meaning they are not tied to a proved figure. The court takes account of the gravity of the imputation, the extent of publication, and the defendant's conduct — including any apology, or its absence.

quiz.q: Which three things must a defamation plaintiff prove?
options: Falsity, malice, damage
Defamatory meaning, reference to the plaintiff, publication
Publication, malice, special damage
Defamatory meaning, malice, damage
quiz.why: Defamatory meaning, reference, publication. Only after all three does any defence arise.
quiz.source: Defamation Act 1957; standard common law elements of the tort

quiz.q: What does 'publication' mean in defamation?
options: Printing in a newspaper
Communication to at least one person other than the plaintiff
Circulation to the public at large
Communication to the plaintiff
quiz.why: One third party is enough. It does not require a newspaper or mass circulation.
quiz.source: Standard common law element; publication is communication to one person other than the plaintiff

quiz.q: Where does malice bite in a defamation action?
options: It is an element of the tort
It defeats justification
It defeats qualified privilege and fair comment
It removes the need to prove publication
quiz.why: Malice is no part of the cause of action. It answers two of the defences and nothing else.
quiz.source: Standard common law; malice defeats qualified privilege and fair comment

quiz.q: What is the effect of s 8 of the Defamation Act 1957?
options: Fair comment needs no factual basis
Justification does not fail merely because every charge is not proved true
Absolute privilege extends to the press
Slander is actionable without proof of damage
quiz.why: It saves the defence where the unproved charges do not materially injure reputation, given the truth of the rest.

quiz.q: Why does the line between libel and slander still matter?
options: Libel carries a criminal penalty
Slander has a longer limitation period
Slander generally requires proof of special damage
Libel cannot be justified
quiz.why: Slander generally needs proof of special damage, subject to the statutory exceptions such as words disparaging a trade.
quiz.source: Defamation Act 1957; slander generally requires proof of special damage

lessons.source: Defamation Act 1957, in particular ss 4, 5, 8 and 9; standard common law elements of the tort.
lessons.verify: Check the current text of the Defamation Act 1957 — section numbering and content should be confirmed — and find current Malaysian authority on the classification of internet publication and on whether Reynolds privilege has been received here.
lessons.plateCaption: The press at work. Publication to one person other than the plaintiff is enough, which is where the tort begins.

lessons.title: Dealings, charges and caveats: how an interest is protected
lessons.summary: Under the Code an interest in land exists when it is registered. Everything else — contracts, caveats, liens — is machinery for getting there, or for stopping somebody else getting there first.

sections.keypoint: An interest in registered land exists on registration, and not before.

body.text: Encik Devan signs the sale and purchase agreement for a shoplot in Seremban and pays the deposit. Does he own it? Not yet.
A dealing is a transaction in registered land — a transfer, a lease, a charge. Under the Code a dealing takes effect at one particular moment, and it is not the moment of signing.
Any dealing under the National Land Code is effective to pass or create an interest in land only upon registration; until then the instrument passes nothing at law.
body.source: National Land Code, Division IV on dealings, read with the registration provisions

body.text: Put simply: the register makes the interest. Until the transfer is registered, the signed document has given Devan nothing at law.
The agreement does give him something. He has a contractual right, and in equity an interest capable of protection. What he does not have is title.
Between signing and registration he is exposed. The whole of the caveat machinery exists because of that gap.
Do not write that a purchaser 'owns' the land on completion of the agreement. The register decides ownership. This is the mistake that unravels an entire answer on priorities.

sections.keypoint: A charge is the Code's security, and where the order for sale goes depends on the kind of title.
sections.h: Charges, and what a chargee may do

body.text: A bank lends RM300,000 against a house. It wants something it can sell if the loan is not repaid.

A charge is the Code's security interest over registered land. It is created by a registered instrument, and it gives the chargee no right of possession. The security is the ability to enforce, not to occupy.
The chargee is the lender who holds the charge. The chargor is the borrower whose land is charged.

items: On default, the chargee serves the statutory notice of default. If the default is not remedied, the chargee may apply for an order for sale.
For land held under **Registry title**, the application goes to the **High Court**.
For land held under **Land Office title**, it goes to the **Land Administrator**.
The court will order a sale unless the chargor shows **cause to the contrary**. That is a narrow concept, not a general discretion to be merciful.

body.text: The Registry-title and Land-Office-title routes are different tracks, with different provisions and different appeal routes. Identify which title the land is held under before you say where the application goes. Getting this wrong is the standard way to go wrong in a charge question.

body.title: Where an order for sale is applied for
body.caption: Identify which title the land is held under before saying where the application goes. This is where the method marks in a charge question sit.
body.alt: A branch on the kind of title. Registry title: the application goes to the High Court, which may order sale on unremedied default. Land Office title: it goes to the Land Administrator, a different track with its own provisions and appeal route.
body.question: Under which title is the land held?

branches.label: The High Court
branches.note: order for sale on unremedied default

branches.label: The Land Administrator
branches.note: a different track, with its own provisions and appeal route

body.q: The borrower defaults. The house is held under Land Office title. Where does the bank apply for an order for sale?
options: The High Court
The Land Administrator
The Sessions Court, because of the amount of the loan
body.why: Land Office title goes to the Land Administrator. Registry title goes to the High Court. What decides it is the class of title, and not the size of the loan. Identify the title before you say where the application goes.

sections.keypoint: A private caveat freezes dealings while a claim is worked out; it creates no interest of its own.

body.text: Devan hears that the seller is showing the same shoplot to another buyer. He cannot stop the seller talking. He can stop the register moving.
Not everybody may lodge a caveat. Section 323 says who may.
A private caveat may be entered by a person claiming title to the land, or claiming any registrable interest in it, or claiming to be beneficially entitled under any trust affecting it.
Put simply: you need a claim to the land itself, or to an interest in it that could be registered, or a beneficial interest under a trust. A grievance on its own is not enough.

body.prompt: Devan lodges a private caveat on the shoplot. What has that given him?
options: An interest in the land, held until the sale goes through
No interest at all — only a block on the register while it stands
First place in the queue, so the land must be transferred to him first
body.reveal: A caveat gives nothing. It stops dealings being registered, which buys time for the claim to be decided. Notice the order: you must already have a claim before you may lodge one. The caveat protects an interest and never creates one. If it felt like staking a claim on the land, that is the misreading the word invites.

body.text: A caveat does not create an interest. It prevents the registration of dealings while it is in force, which buys time for the claim to be determined.
It lapses after the statutory period unless it is extended. A person aggrieved by it may apply to have it removed.

On such an application the caveator must show two things. First, that the claim discloses a serious question to be tried. Second, that the balance of convenience favours maintaining the caveat until trial.
That is the same shape as the test for an interlocutory injunction, and it is that shape for the same reason. The court is holding the position without deciding the fight.
A caveat entered without reasonable cause exposes the caveator to compensation. It is not a costless holding move. Advising a client to lodge one 'just in case' is advice with a price attached.

sections.keypoint: Registrar's, lien-holder's and trust caveats — and a deposited title document points at the second.

items: **Registrar's caveat** — entered by the Registrar to protect the interests of the Federation or a State, or of a person under disability, or to prevent fraud or improper dealing.
**Lien-holder's caveat** — where the issue document of title is deposited as security for a loan, this is how the lender protects it. The lien becomes enforceable once the caveat is entered.
**Trust caveat** — protecting land held on trust.

body.text: A question that mentions a deposited title document is almost always a lien-holder's caveat question. Spotting it by that cue is faster than reasoning from first principles.

sections.keypoint: Section 340 and deferred indefeasibility are what answer the forged-transfer worry.

body.text: Registration is powerful, and that raises an obvious worry. What if somebody forges your signature and registers a transfer of your land?

Section 340 gives the registered proprietor an indefeasible title — a registered title that cannot be set aside. Section 340(2) then lists the exceptions, which include fraud and a void or forged instrument.

*Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San* restored deferred indefeasibility. A person who acquires title through a void or forged instrument does not obtain an indefeasible title. A later purchaser in good faith and for value may.

*Adorna Properties Sdn Bhd v Boonsom Boonyanit* held the opposite, and it stood for nine years. If a source you are reading relies on it without noting that it was departed from, stop trusting that source.

quiz.q: When does a dealing pass an interest in registered land?
options: On execution of the instrument
On registration
On payment of the price
On delivery of the title document
quiz.why: The register creates the interest. Everything before registration is contractual or equitable only.
quiz.source: National Land Code; an interest in registered land passes on registration

quiz.q: What does a private caveat actually do?
options: Creates an interest in the land
Prevents registration of dealings while it is in force
Transfers beneficial ownership
Operates as a charge
quiz.why: It is a freeze, not an interest. It buys time for the underlying claim to be determined.

quiz.q: On an application to remove a private caveat, what must the caveator show?
options: A serious question to be tried, and that the balance of convenience favours the caveat
That he will succeed at trial
That he has registered title
That the registered proprietor consents
quiz.why: The same shape as an interlocutory injunction test, because the court is holding the position, not deciding it.
quiz.source: National Land Code, the caveat provisions (ss 320-330)

quiz.q: A chargee wants an order for sale of land held under Registry title. Where does the application go?
options: The Land Administrator
The Sessions Court
The Registrar of Titles
The High Court
quiz.why: Registry title goes to the High Court. Land Office title goes to the Land Administrator.
quiz.source: National Land Code, the charge and order-for-sale provisions

quiz.q: Which case restored deferred indefeasibility under s 340?
options: Adorna Properties v Boonsom Boonyanit
Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San
Cubic Electronics v Mars
Kepong Prospecting v Schmidt
quiz.why: Tan Ying Hong departed from Adorna Properties, which had held for immediate indefeasibility.
quiz.source: Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San [2010] 2 MLJ 1 (FC); Adorna Properties Sdn Bhd v Boonsom Boonyanit [2001] 1 MLJ 241 (FC)

quiz.q: The facts mention an issue document of title deposited as security. Which caveat is in issue?
options: A private caveat
A Registrar's caveat
A trust caveat
A lien-holder's caveat
quiz.why: Deposit of the title document, plus an intention to secure, is the lien-holder's caveat cue.
quiz.source: National Land Code, the caveat provisions (ss 320-330)

lessons.title: Directors' duties, and what a member can do about a breach
lessons.summary: The Companies Act 2016 states the duties in statute. The remedies — oppression, the statutory derivative action, and winding up on the just and equitable ground — belong to different people and answer different complaints.

sections.keypoint: Proper purpose, good faith, best interest of the company — plus reasonable care, skill and diligence.

body.text: Three friends set up a company to run a car wash. One of them is the director who signs everything. He quietly buys the soap and the brushes from his brother's firm, at twice the going price.
A director holds power over property that is not his own. The Companies Act 2016 says how that power must be used.
A director shall at all times exercise his powers in accordance with this Act, for a proper purpose and in good faith in the best interest of the company.
Put simply: use your powers for the purpose they were given, honestly, and for the company rather than for yourself.
That is a fiduciary duty in statutory form. Fiduciary means an obligation of loyalty owed by somebody trusted to act for another.
Loyalty is one thing. Competence is another, and the next subsection deals with it.

A director shall exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence with the knowledge, skill and experience which may reasonably be expected of a director having the same responsibilities, and any additional knowledge, skill and experience which the director in fact has.
Put simply: a director must take the care an ordinary director in his position would take. If he happens to be an accountant or an engineer, more is expected of him, because he knows more.
Section 218 deals separately with the improper use of the company's property, position or information.
Section 214 provides a shelter, called the business judgement rule. A director who makes a business judgement in good faith and for a proper purpose is taken to have met section 213(2).

That shelter comes with conditions. He must have no material personal interest in the subject matter. He must inform himself on a reasonable basis. And he must reasonably believe the judgement is in the best interest of the company.
The shelter covers the duty of care in s 213(2). It does not cover the fiduciary duty in s 213(1). A director who helps himself cannot answer with a business judgement.

sections.keypoint: A loss suffered by the company is the company's to sue on, even when every member feels it.

body.text: The car wash loses RM80,000 through the overpriced supplies. The other two friends watch the value of their shares fall. Can they sue the director for that fall?

body.prompt: The car wash is RM80,000 poorer and the two friends watch their shares lose value. Can they sue the director for what their shares lost?
options: Yes — it is their money that has gone
No — the loss belongs to the company
Yes, if between them they hold more than half the shares
body.reveal: Usually not. The company is a person in law, separate from its members, and the wrong was done to it. The fall in their shares only reflects the company's loss. The first answer is how this feels from the inside, and that is why the rule has to be met head on. They are not left without a remedy: the routes come next.

body.text: Usually not, and this is what catches people out. The wrong was done to the company, and a company is a person in law separate from its members. A wrong done to the company is the company's to complain of.
The company acts through its board, or through its members in general meeting. Where the board is the wrongdoer, that is precisely the problem the law has to solve.

The most common error is to reach for a derivative action or an oppression petition without first asking who suffered the loss. A fall in the value of every member's shares because the company was harmed is reflective loss. It is the company's claim, not the member's.

body.title: Ask who suffered the loss, before anything else
body.caption: A fall in the value of every member's shares because the company was harmed is reflective loss. Reaching for a route before answering this question is the commonest error in the area.
body.alt: A question — who actually suffered the loss? — branching two ways. The company: the claim is the company's to bring, and a fall in every member's shares is merely reflective of it. The member personally: the wrong was done to them rather than to the company, and the claim is their own.
body.question: Who actually suffered the loss?

branches.label: The company's claim
branches.note: a fall in every member's shares is reflective

branches.label: The member's own claim
branches.note: a wrong to them, not to the company

sections.keypoint: Oppression, the statutory derivative action, or winding up — and each answers a different complaint.

body.text: There are three main routes, and each answers a different complaint. Choosing between them is most of the analysis in a problem question.

items: **Oppression (s 346).** A member may complain that the affairs of the company are being conducted, or the directors' powers exercised, in a manner oppressive to members or in disregard of their interests. The complaint is about how *he* has been treated. The court's powers on such a petition are wide.

**Statutory derivative action (ss 347 to 350).** A member, a director or the Registrar may bring proceedings **on behalf of the company**, to enforce the company's own right. It requires the **leave of the court** — the court's permission to proceed. The applicant must show good faith, and that the action is prima facie in the company's best interest.

**Winding up on the just and equitable ground.** The court may wind the company up where it is just and equitable to do so. It is used most often in a quasi-partnership, where a small company was really a partnership and the trust between the members has broken down. It is the remedy of last resort, and it kills the company.

body.text: Back to the car wash. If the complaint is that the company was drained of RM80,000, the loss is the company's and the route is a derivative action. If the complaint is that the two friends were shut out of meetings, refused the accounts and cut off from any dividend, that is about their own treatment. The route there is oppression.
An oppression petition and a derivative action are not alternatives to be pleaded together without thought. They proceed on inconsistent premises about whose right is being vindicated.

body.caption: An oppression petition and a derivative action are not alternatives to plead together. They rest on inconsistent premises about whose right is being vindicated.
rows: The company was drained of RM80,000
The company's — brought on its behalf
I was shut out of meetings and refused the accounts
The relationship this company rested on has broken down
Winding up on the just and equitable ground

sections.keypoint: The company is a separate person, and courts look behind that rarely and on stated grounds.
sections.h: Separate legal personality, and its limits

body.text: A company incorporated under the Act is a body corporate with its own legal personality. It can own property, owe money, and sue and be sued in its own name.
Its debts are not its members' debts. That is the foundation of everything above, and of *Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd*.
Courts do sometimes look behind the company at the people running it. That is called lifting the corporate veil, and it is done rarely and on stated grounds.
Those grounds are fraud, the use of the corporate form as a device to evade an existing obligation, or a statute that so provides.
Section 540 of the Act is a statutory route of that kind. Where the business has been carried on to defraud creditors, those knowingly party to it may be made personally liable.

'Lifting the veil in the interests of justice' is not a ground, however often it is asserted. Check the current Malaysian authority before advancing it, and prefer a statutory route where one is available.

body.q: When will a court look behind a company at the people running it?
options: Whenever it would be unjust not to
On stated grounds — fraud, evading an existing obligation, or where a statute provides
Whenever the company cannot pay its debts
body.why: The grounds are narrow and the courts use them rarely. 'In the interests of justice' is asserted constantly and is not a ground. A company that cannot pay is the ordinary case, not a reason to reach its members. Prefer a statutory route, such as section 540, where one is available.

sections.keypoint: The 2016 Act removed the mandatory AGM for private companies and allows written resolutions.

body.text: The Act removed the mandatory annual general meeting for private companies, and provides for written resolutions instead. Public companies must still hold an AGM.

Notice periods, quorum, and the distinction between ordinary and special resolutions are governed by the Act and by the constitution. Quorum is the minimum attendance a meeting needs in order to be valid.
A procedural irregularity may be cured, or it may invalidate the resolution. Which of those happens depends on the provision engaged.
This is an area where the 2016 Act changed the law substantially from the Companies Act 1965. Treat any source written before 2017 as describing a repealed statute until you have checked it.

quiz.q: Which provision states the duty to act in good faith in the best interest of the company?
options: Section 214
Section 218
Section 346
Section 213(1)
quiz.why: Section 213(1) is the fiduciary duty in statutory form. Section 213(2) is the separate duty of care.

quiz.q: Directors have harmed the company, and every member's shares are worth less. What is the difficulty with a member suing personally?
options: Members may never sue directors
The loss is reflective; the claim belongs to the company
The claim is time-barred
Only the Registrar may sue
quiz.why: A wrong to the company is the company's to complain of. That is why the derivative action machinery exists.
quiz.source: Companies Act 2016 ss 347-350; a wrong to the company is the company's to complain of

quiz.q: What does a statutory derivative action require?
options: Leave of the court, good faith, and that it is prima facie in the company's best interest
A special resolution
The consent of the board
A prior oppression petition
quiz.why: Sections 347 to 350 set out the leave requirement and the criteria for granting it.

quiz.q: Which remedy answers a complaint about how a member has been treated?
options: A derivative action
Fraudulent trading under s 540
Rectification of the register
Oppression under s 346
quiz.why: Section 346 is about the conduct of the company's affairs in a manner oppressive to a member.

quiz.q: What does the business judgement rule in s 214 do?
options: Deems the duty of care met where its conditions are satisfied
Excuses breaches of fiduciary duty
Applies only to executive directors
Removes the duty of care for private companies
quiz.why: It is a safe harbour for s 213(2) only. It does not shelter the fiduciary duty in s 213(1).

quiz.q: Why should a company law book published in 2015 be treated with care?
options: The 1965 Act is still in force alongside the 2016 Act
Company law is a State matter
The Companies Act 2016 substantially changed the law
Older reports are unreliable
quiz.why: The 1965 Act was repealed. A pre-2017 text is describing a repealed statute until you have checked it.
quiz.source: Companies Act 2016 (Act 777), which repealed the Companies Act 1965

reading.where: the annotations to ss 213, 214, 218, 346 and 347-350

lessons.source: Companies Act 2016 ss 213, 214, 218, 346, 347-350, 540; Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd [1897] AC 22.
lessons.verify: Check every section number against the current text of Act 777, and check the current Malaysian authority on lifting the corporate veil and on the leave criteria for a statutory derivative action before relying on the summary above.
lessons.plateCaption: A member outvoted. Whose right was hurt — the company's or the member's own — decides which of the three remedies fits.

lessons.title: Burden and standard of proof under the Evidence Act
lessons.summary: Sections 101 to 106 distribute the burden. They separate the burden of proof from the burden of adducing evidence, and a great deal turns on which one a provision is talking about.

sections.keypoint: Section 101 is the legal burden and it does not shift; section 103 is the evidential one and it does.

body.text: Two people give different accounts of the same events and there is no CCTV. Somebody has to lose. The Evidence Act 1950 decides who.
Section 101 sets out the basic idea and gives it a name.

Whoever desires any court to give judgment as to any legal right or liability, dependent on the existence of facts which he asserts, must prove that those facts exist. When a person is bound to prove the existence of any fact, it is said that the burden of proof lies on that person.
Put simply: if you want the court to act on a fact, it is your job to prove it. That job is called the burden of proof.
Section 102 answers a different question. Who is carrying that burden in this particular case?
The burden of proof in a suit or proceeding lies on that person who would fail if no evidence at all were given on either side.
Put simply: imagine that neither side calls a single witness. Whoever loses in that imaginary case is the one carrying the burden.
What sections 101 and 102 describe is the legal burden. That is the risk of losing if the fact is not proved, and it does not shift.
Section 103 is doing something else. It places the burden of proving any particular fact on the person who wishes the court to believe it.
That is the evidential burden — the burden of putting enough evidence on a point to make it live. Unlike the legal burden, it does shift as the case proceeds.

Puan Chin sues over an unpaid loan of RM8,000. If neither side calls any evidence she loses, so the legal burden is hers. She produces the bank transfer and a message promising repayment. In practice the defendant must now answer. That is the evidential burden moving, not the legal one.

Answers routinely say 'the burden shifted to the defendant' when they mean the evidential burden. Say which one you mean. The legal burden in a criminal case shifts only where a statute makes it shift.

body.caption: Which burden a provision is talking about
rows: s 102 — who would fail on a blank record
Yes, as the evidence goes in
Legal, **on the accused**, on the balance of probabilities
s 106 — a fact especially within knowledge

body.q: Puan Chin produces the bank transfer and the message promising repayment. In practice the defendant must now answer. Which burden has moved?
options: The legal burden — the defendant must now prove he repaid
The evidential burden — the legal burden stays with her
Both, because she has proved her case
body.why: The legal burden is the risk of losing if a fact is not proved, and it does not shift. What moved is the practical need to answer. Writing 'the burden shifted' without saying which one is the routine error.

sections.keypoint: Section 105 puts a real legal burden on an accused relying on a general exception.

body.text: Section 105 is one of those statutes, and it was met in the criminal law module.

It places on the accused the burden of proving circumstances that bring the case within a general exception in the Penal Code. It does the same for any special exception or proviso in the law defining the offence. It also directs the court to presume the absence of those circumstances.
That is a genuine legal burden on the accused, discharged on the balance of probabilities. It is the principal statutory exception to the rule that the prosecution proves everything.

sections.keypoint: Section 106 reaches one fact peculiarly within someone's knowledge — it cannot reverse the case.
sections.h: Facts only one person can know

body.text: A man is found riding a motorcycle that was reported stolen. Asked where he got it, he says nothing. Who has to prove what?

body.prompt: The motorcycle was reported stolen and he is riding it. He will not say where he got it. Who has to prove where it came from?
options: The prosecution — it has to prove its whole case
The rider, because that fact sits with him alone
Nobody; saying nothing proves nothing either way
body.reveal: Section 106 puts it on the rider. Where a fact is known to one person and nobody else, that person has to prove it. Keep the first answer too. It stays true of the case as a whole, and the caution below is about how often section 106 is stretched past this point.

body.text: When any fact is especially within the knowledge of any person, the burden of proving that fact is upon him.
Put simply: where a fact sits with one person and with nobody else, that person has to prove it.
The point of the section is practical. A licence, an authority, a reason for being somewhere — these sit with one person. It would be unreasonable to make the other side prove a negative about them.

Section 106 is the most over-used provision in the Act. It does not relieve the prosecution of proving its case. It applies to a specific fact peculiarly within a person's knowledge, and it cannot be used to reverse the general burden. An answer that deploys s 106 to shift the whole case has misread it.

sections.keypoint: May presume, shall presume, conclusive proof: three different strengths, and the Act picks deliberately.

body.text: A presumption is a direction about what the court may or must infer. Section 4 defines three strengths of it.

items: **May presume** — the court has a discretion. It may treat the fact as proved, or it may call for proof of it.
**Shall presume** — the court must treat the fact as proved, unless and until it is disproved.
**Conclusive proof** — the fact is settled, and no evidence to the contrary is allowed.

body.text: Section 114 lists facts the court may presume. Illustration (g) is the one that appears constantly. Evidence which could be produced and is not would, if produced, be unfavourable to the person who withholds it.
A driver's dashcam was working on the day of the crash, and he does not produce the footage. The other side asks the court to infer that it would not have helped him. That is illustration (g).

Illustration (g) is permissive, and it is not drawn automatically from every gap in the evidence. The party inviting the inference must show that the evidence was available and material, and that no explanation for its absence has been given.

sections.keypoint: None of it arises until the evidence is admissible, and relevance is defined by the Act.

body.text: None of this arises until the evidence is admissible. Section 5 admits evidence of facts in issue and of relevant facts, and relevance is defined by the Act rather than at large.
A fact is not admissible because it is interesting, or because it sounds probative, or because it seems fair to admit it. It is admissible because a section makes it relevant.
Keep the two questions apart in writing. First: is this admissible under a named section? Second: who has to prove what, and to what standard? Merging them is the fastest way to a confused answer.

quiz.q: Which section says the burden lies on the person who would fail if no evidence were given?
options: Section 101
Section 103
Section 102
Section 106
quiz.why: Section 102 identifies who carries the legal burden by asking who loses on a blank record.

quiz.q: What is the effect of s 105 on an accused relying on a general exception?
options: He carries an evidential burden only
The prosecution must disprove it beyond reasonable doubt
The exception is presumed in his favour
He carries a legal burden, on the balance of probabilities
quiz.why: The court presumes the circumstances are absent, and the accused must prove them.

quiz.q: What is the correct scope of s 106?
options: A specific fact especially within a person's knowledge
The whole of the defence case
Any fact the prosecution cannot easily prove
All facts occurring in private
quiz.why: One specific fact peculiarly within a person's knowledge. It cannot be used to reverse the general burden.

quiz.q: What does 'shall presume' mean under s 4?
options: The court may treat the fact as proved
No evidence in rebuttal is allowed
The fact is admitted
The court must treat the fact as proved unless it is disproved
quiz.why: 'May presume' is a discretion, and 'conclusive proof' admits no rebuttal at all.

quiz.q: When may an adverse inference be drawn under illustration (g) to s 114?
options: From any gap in the evidence
Whenever a witness is not called
Automatically against the defence
Where material evidence was available, withheld, and unexplained
quiz.why: It is permissive and conditional, not a default the court applies to every gap.

quiz.q: What must be established before any question of burden arises?
options: That the witness is credible
That the parties agree
That the evidence is admissible under a named section
That the fact is important
quiz.why: Relevancy is the gate, and it is defined by the Act rather than left at large.
quiz.source: Evidence Act 1950, Part I; relevancy is the gate

reading.where: the chapters on burden of proof and presumptions
for the treatment of ss 101-106

lessons.verify: Check the sections against the current text of Act 56, and check current authority on the conditions for drawing an adverse inference under s 114(g) — it is frequently argued and the formulations differ.
lessons.plateCaption: The two standards on one beam. Section 105 is the main statutory exception to the rule that the prosecution proves everything.

lessons.title: Ending a case early, and holding the position meanwhile
lessons.summary: Most civil cases never reach trial. Order 14, Order 18 rule 19 and Order 29 of the Rules of Court 2012 are how they end, and each has a different threshold.

sections.keypoint: Order 14 asks whether there is a triable issue, not whether the defence would win.

body.text: A supplier is owed RM60,000 on invoices the buyer signed for. The buyer files a defence saying only that he disputes the sum. Must the supplier wait two years for a trial?
Not necessarily. A plaintiff who says the defence is hopeless may apply for judgment without a trial. That is Order 14.
The application is supported by affidavit — a written statement sworn to be true. It verifies the facts and states a belief that there is no defence.

body.prompt: The buyer's defence says only that he disputes the sum. What does he have to show to stop judgment being entered now, without a trial?
options: That his defence will probably succeed at trial
That there is an issue in dispute which ought to be tried
That the supplier cannot prove the debt
body.reveal: He only has to show there is something worth trying. The court is not asking who would win. A defence that is thin but not hopeless may still get him in, on conditions such as paying money into court. If you expected him to show a good defence, you are in good company. Weighing the merits as though at trial is the standard way to get this wrong.

body.text: The defendant resists by showing an issue or question in dispute which ought to be tried, or that there ought for some other reason to be a trial. Where he does, unconditional leave to defend follows; where the defence is shadowy, leave may be conditional.
Put simply: the defendant does not have to win. He has to show there is something worth trying. A defence that is thin but not hopeless may get him in on conditions, such as paying money into court.
The threshold is not whether the defence will succeed. It is whether there is a triable issue, and an answer that weighs the merits as if at trial has applied the wrong test.

body.title: Two applications that look alike and are not

items: Says: the defence has no substance **on the evidence**.
Affidavits go in on both sides.
Threshold: is there a triable issue? Not, would the defence win.
A shadowy defence may get conditional leave to defend.
Says: the pleading is bad **as a document**.
On the no-reasonable-cause-of-action limb, no evidence is admissible at all.
The pleaded facts are assumed true.
Used sparingly, and only in plain and obvious cases.

sections.keypoint: Order 18 rule 19 attacks the pleading as a document, and on one limb no evidence is admissible at all.

body.text: Sometimes the problem is not the evidence. It is the document itself.
A pleading is the document setting out a party's case in material facts — the statement of claim, or the defence.

items: The court may strike out a pleading which discloses no reasonable cause of action or defence.
It may also strike out one that is scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, or that may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial, or that is otherwise an abuse of process.
On the first ground no evidence is admissible. The question is taken on the pleading as it stands.
The jurisdiction is used sparingly, and only in plain and obvious cases. A difficult point of law is not by itself a reason to strike out.

body.text: The distinction from Order 14 is worth stating. Order 14 says the defence has no substance on the evidence. Order 18 rule 19 says the pleading is bad as a document.

sections.keypoint: Serious question, damages inadequate, balance of convenience — plus an undertaking in damages.

body.text: A landlord starts clearing a tenant's stock out of a shoplot while the dispute over the tenancy is still running. By the time a trial comes, the stock will be gone.
An injunction is a court order to do something, or to stop doing something. An interlocutory injunction is one that holds the position until trial.

The applicant must show a serious question to be tried; that damages would not be an adequate remedy; and that the balance of convenience lies in favour of granting the injunction. An undertaking in damages is ordinarily required.
body.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 29; Keet Gerald Francis Noel John v Mohd Noor bin Abdullah [1995] 1 MLJ 193 (CA), applying American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd [1975] AC 396

body.text: Put simply: show there is a real dispute worth trying. Show that money paid afterwards would not put it right. Show that holding the position does less harm than not holding it.
The undertaking in damages is a promise to compensate the other side if the order turns out to have been wrongly granted. It is not a formality.
The Malaysian courts have their own gloss on this. The case to cite is *Keet Gerald Francis Noel John v Mohd Noor bin Abdullah* [1995] 1 MLJ 193, a Court of Appeal decision.

It asks the judge to find a *bona fide* serious question to be tried, rather than merely a question that is not frivolous. The judge does not weigh the merits at this stage. He then asks where the justice of the case lies, setting the harm an injunction would do against the harm of refusing it.
An *ex parte* application is one made without notice to the other side. There the duty of full and frank disclosure is strict, and a breach of it is itself a ground for discharge.
A mandatory interlocutory injunction — one requiring something to be done rather than restrained — attracts a higher threshold. Identify which kind you are asking for before you state the test.

sections.keypoint: The strongest claim is worth nothing brought too late, and limitation must be pleaded.
sections.h: Limitation, which decides more cases than any of these

body.text: The strongest claim in the world is worth nothing if it is brought too late.
The Limitation Act 1953 sets six years for actions founded on contract or on tort. Time runs from the date on which the cause of action accrued.
Different periods apply to actions to recover land and to certain other claims. There are also provisions on disability, on acknowledgment, and on part payment.

Limitation is a defence that must be pleaded, and a court will not take the point for a defendant who has not. Check the current text of the Act for the period applicable to the particular claim. Check also whether a special limitation provision in another statute displaces it.

body.title: Limitation periods, by kind of claim

data.label: Tort
data.note: generally runs from when damage occurs, not from the act

body.caption: Years from the accrual of the cause of action. Accrual is not the same as the wrongful act — in contract it runs from breach, in negligence generally from damage.
body.source: Limitation Act 1953. Check the current text for the period applicable to the particular claim.
body.note: Other statutes contain their own, shorter periods, and limitation is a defence that must be pleaded — a court will not take the point for a defendant who has not.

body.q: A contract claim is filed eight years after the breach. The defendant's lawyer says nothing about the delay. What should the court do?
options: Refuse the claim; the period for a contract claim is six years
Hear it — limitation is a defence and it has to be pleaded
Ask the defendant whether he wants to rely on limitation
body.why: The claim is out of time. But the time bar is a defence, and the court will not take the point for a defendant who has not raised it. The first answer treats limitation as something the court polices by itself. Check as well whether another statute sets a special period.

sections.keypoint: Judgment is a right to be paid; enforcement is a separate exercise with its own procedures.

body.text: Winning is one step. Getting paid is another one.

Enforcement is a separate exercise with its own procedures. There is a writ of seizure and sale, and there are garnishee proceedings, which capture money that others owe the debtor. There is a judgment debtor summons, and a charging order. And there is winding up or bankruptcy, where the debtor simply cannot pay.
An advice that stops at 'the plaintiff will obtain judgment' has stopped one step early.

quiz.q: What must a defendant show to resist summary judgment under Order 14?
options: That the defence will succeed
A triable issue, or some other reason for a trial
That the plaintiff acted in bad faith
That the claim is time-barred
quiz.why: A triable issue, or some other reason for a trial. Not that the defence will actually succeed.

quiz.q: On an application to strike out for disclosing no reasonable cause of action, what evidence is admissible?
options: Affidavit evidence from both sides
None — the pleading is taken as it stands
The documents only
Oral evidence
quiz.why: Under that limb of O 18 r 19 the question is decided on the pleading alone.

quiz.q: Which of these is *not* part of the interlocutory injunction test?
options: Adequacy of damages
A serious question to be tried
Whether the applicant will probably win at trial
Balance of convenience
quiz.why: The court does not try the merits at the interlocutory stage. It holds the position until trial.
quiz.source: Keet Gerald Francis Noel John v Mohd Noor bin Abdullah [1995] 1 MLJ 193 (CA); American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd [1975] AC 396

quiz.q: What is the special obligation on an ex parte application?
options: A larger undertaking in damages
Service on the defendant first
Full and frank disclosure
Leave of a judge in chambers
quiz.why: Full and frank disclosure. Breaking it is itself a ground for discharging the order.
quiz.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 29; the duty of full and frank disclosure on an ex parte application

quiz.q: What is the general limitation period for an action founded on contract or tort?
options: Three years
Twelve years
Six years from accrual
Six years from discovery
quiz.why: Six years from accrual, subject to the special periods and to any statute that displaces the Act.

quiz.q: Why is 'the plaintiff will obtain judgment' an incomplete advice?
options: Enforcement is a separate exercise
Judgments are not final
Appeals are automatic
Costs are not included
quiz.why: A judgment is a right to be paid, not payment. The enforcement route has to be advised on too.
quiz.source: Rules of Court 2012; enforcement is a separate exercise from obtaining judgment

Keet Gerald is the Malaysian decision to cite for the interlocutory injunction test, and its citation should be confirmed in a report you can hold. The local gloss on American Cyanamid is stated differently in different judgments, so check for later Federal Court authority before relying on the formulation above.

lessons.title: Fair procedure, legitimate expectation, and the limits of review
lessons.summary: Procedural impropriety is the ground most often made out and most often pleaded badly. The two rules are old, narrow and precise, and legitimate expectation extends them only so far.

sections.keypoint: A licence cancelled by letter, with no reason and no chance to answer — two rules, not a general power.
sections.h: Two rules, not a general power

body.text: A hawker in Klang opens a letter. Her licence is cancelled from today. No reason is given, and nobody asked her anything.
Whatever the council's reasons, something has already gone wrong. Two rules govern how a decision like that must be made.
They are old, narrow and precise. They are not a general power for a judge to do whatever seems fair.

items: **Hear the other side.** A person liable to be affected by a decision must be given notice of the case against him, and a fair opportunity to answer it. What that requires varies with the decision. An oral hearing is not always necessary, reasons are not always required, and legal representation is not always allowed.

**Nobody may be a judge in his own cause.** Actual bias is rare and hard to prove. The working test is objective: would a fair-minded and informed observer conclude that there was a real danger, or a real possibility, of bias?

body.text: The Latin names for the two are *audi alteram partem* and *nemo judex in causa sua*. Together they are called natural justice, or procedural fairness.

Check which formulation of the bias test the Malaysian courts currently apply, and cite a Malaysian decision for it. 'Real danger' and 'real possibility' have both been used, and the difference matters.

sections.keypoint: How much process is due varies with what is at stake and with the statutory scheme.

body.text: The rules apply almost everywhere. How much they demand varies a great deal.
Three things drive it. What is at stake for the person. What the empowering statute says. And what kind of decision it is.
A decision affecting livelihood or liberty attracts more. A preliminary or investigatory step, which decides nothing yet, attracts less.

The hawker's licence is revoked without warning, and without her being told what she is said to have done. That is a straightforward case of not being heard. Now change it. She is heard, makes her representations in person, but is refused legal representation. That is arguable, and the argument is about content, not existence.
So say what these facts required, and why. Asserting that 'natural justice applies' has not decided anything.

sections.keypoint: A clear representation or a settled practice can found an expectation — procedurally, at least.

body.text: A department has renewed a permit every year for eleven years. It has said in writing that holders will be consulted before the scheme changes. This year the scheme changes overnight.
Nobody has a right to a permit. But a clear and unambiguous representation, or a settled practice, can create an expectation the law will protect. Lawyers call it a legitimate expectation.
It is most secure as a **procedural** expectation — that the person will be consulted, or heard, before a change. That is what the writing promised here.
A **substantive** legitimate expectation is the harder claim: that the benefit itself will be conferred. It is more contested.
Its reception in Malaysia should be checked against current authority before it is asserted. An answer that treats it as settled is overstating the position.

An expectation cannot be legitimate if the representation was outside the decision-maker's power. A public body cannot bind itself to act unlawfully, and an answer that overlooks that has usually reached the wrong conclusion.

body.q: The department promised in writing to consult permit holders before changing the scheme, then changed it overnight. What can a holder claim?
options: That the change is void and the old permits continue
That he should have been consulted first
Nothing — nobody has a right to a permit
body.why: The promise was about being consulted, so the expectation it created is a procedural one. That is the form the law protects most securely. The last answer confuses having no right to the benefit with having no claim at all. The first is the substantive version, which is harder and should be checked against current authority.

sections.keypoint: Illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety, with proportionality argued as a fourth.

body.text: Procedural fairness is one ground among several. Judicial review is the court reviewing how a public decision was made, not whether it was right.

items: **Illegality** — the decision-maker misdirected itself in law, or acted outside its powers. Or it took into account irrelevant considerations, failed to take into account relevant ones, or acted for an improper purpose.
**Irrationality** — a decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have come to it. The bar is high.
**Procedural impropriety** — the two rules above, and failure to observe a mandatory procedural requirement in the empowering statute.

**Proportionality** — asking whether a restriction goes further than its purpose requires. It is accepted in Malaysia in the constitutional context. Whether it stands as a free-standing head of administrative review should be checked rather than assumed.

body.prompt: The hawker takes the council to court over her cancelled licence, and she wins. What does the court give her?
options: Her licence back
The cancellation quashed, and the council free to decide again
Compensation for the trading days she lost
body.reveal: The court quashes the decision. It is reviewing how the decision was made, not whether she should keep her licence. The council may take the decision again, this time after hearing her, and it may lawfully reach the same result. Winning and getting nothing back feels like a poor sort of victory, and that feeling is the clearest way to remember what judicial review is.

body.text: Review is of the decision-making process, not of the merits. The court is not asking whether it would have decided the same way.

The Malaysian courts have gone further than the English in places. There is authority allowing a court to substitute its own decision in an appropriate case, rather than remitting the matter. Cite that line of authority if you rely on it.

sections.keypoint: Order 53 has its own gate: leave, standing, and a time limit that correspondence does not stop.

body.text: Getting the law right is not enough. Judicial review has its own gate, and it is easy to walk into.

items: An application for judicial review is made under Order 53 of the Rules of Court 2012.
It requires **leave** — the court's permission to bring the application at all.
There is a time limit. The application for leave must be made promptly, and within the period prescribed by the rule, running from the date when the grounds arose.
The applicant must be **adversely affected** by the decision. The Malaysian test for standing has been stated in the Federal Court, and it is narrower than the English 'sufficient interest'.

The relief includes certiorari, which quashes a decision, prohibition, which forbids one, and mandamus, which compels a public duty to be performed. A declaration and an injunction are also available, and damages may be claimed in the same proceedings where the rule allows.

body.text: Getting the procedure wrong ends the case regardless of its merits. Check the current Order 53 text for the time limit and the leave requirement before advising on any application.

body.title: Order 53, in the order the obstacles arrive

items.text: The application for leave must be made within the period the rule prescribes, running from when the grounds arose. Correspondence with the decision-maker does not stop time.
A threshold the court can refuse without reaching the merits.
The applicant must be *adversely affected* — the Malaysian test, narrower than the English sufficient interest.
Illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety; proportionality argued as a fourth.
Certiorari to quash, and remitter for reconsideration by a differently constituted body. Not usually an order that the applicant wins.

quiz.q: What does audi alteram partem require?
options: An oral hearing in every case
Legal representation in every case
Notice of the case and a fair opportunity to answer it
Written reasons in every case
quiz.why: Notice of the case and a fair opportunity to answer it. The content varies with the decision.
quiz.source: Standard common law rule of natural justice; audi alteram partem

quiz.q: Which is the practical test for bias?
options: Whether the applicant felt aggrieved
Whether the decision-maker was actually biased
Whether the decision was wrong
Whether a fair-minded and informed observer would see a real danger or possibility of bias
quiz.why: Actual bias is rarely provable, so the objective test does the work. Check which formulation Malaysia currently uses.
quiz.source: Standard common law test for apparent bias; the current Malaysian formulation should be checked

quiz.q: Which form of legitimate expectation is the more secure?
options: Procedural — that the person will be heard before a change
Whichever one the applicant relied on to his detriment
Substantive — that the benefit will be conferred
One created by the empowering statute itself
quiz.why: The substantive form is more contested, and its reception in Malaysia should be checked rather than assumed.
quiz.source: The Malaysian authorities on legitimate expectation; the substantive form is contested

quiz.q: A public body promises to act in a way the statute does not permit. Can a legitimate expectation arise?
options: Yes, if the representation was clear
Yes, if the applicant relied on it
No — a body cannot bind itself to act unlawfully
Only if the representation was in writing
quiz.why: An expectation founded on something outside the decision-maker's power cannot be legitimate.
quiz.source: Standard common law; an expectation founded on something outside the decision-maker's power cannot be legitimate

quiz.q: What must an applicant for judicial review under Order 53 obtain first?
options: Leave of the court
A declaration
An undertaking in damages
The consent of the decision-maker
quiz.why: Leave — the court's permission. The application must also be made within the prescribed time.

quiz.q: What is the Malaysian standing requirement for judicial review?
options: Sufficient interest, as in England
Any member of the public may apply
That the applicant is adversely affected by the decision
Only a party to the original proceedings
quiz.why: That the applicant is adversely affected. It has been stated in the Federal Court and is narrower than the English test.
quiz.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 53; the applicant must be adversely affected

Wade and Forsyth is English and states English law.
lessons.plateCaption: A hearing with one chair empty. The commonest ground, and the one most often pleaded without saying what fairness required on these facts.

lessons.title: Getting a decision into court
lessons.summary: Judicial review has a doorway before it has an argument. Leave, time, standing and the right remedy are decided first, and most challenges that fail never reach a ground at all.

sections.keypoint: Judicial review starts with an application for leave, decided before the merits.

body.text: A council refuses Encik Bakri a hawker licence. He believes the refusal was unlawful and wants a court to say so.
He cannot simply sue. Judicial review runs through a particular procedure, and the first step is asking the court for leave to bring it.
An application for judicial review shall not be made unless leave has been granted. The application for leave must be made promptly and within the time the Rules prescribe.
Leave is a filter, not a hearing. It asks whether the case is arguable and whether the applicant should be allowed to bring it.
Time runs from the decision, not from when the applicant learned it was arguable. Delay defeats more reviews than any ground succeeds on.

sections.keypoint: Standing asks whether this applicant is the right person to complain.
sections.h: Whether it is your complaint to make

body.text: Public law is not open to everybody who disagrees. The applicant must have a sufficient interest in the matter.
Bakri plainly has one. The decision was about his licence.
The harder cases are the ones brought by somebody affected indirectly: a neighbour, a rival trader, an association speaking for members.
The court shall not grant leave unless it considers that the applicant has a sufficient interest in the matter to which the application relates.
Standing is decided at leave, which is why it comes before anything about legality.

sections.keypoint: The remedies are separate orders, and they do different jobs.

body.text: Naming the remedy is part of the pleading. Ask for the wrong one and the right argument achieves nothing.

body.caption: The orders, and what each one does
rows: Stops a body from acting or continuing to act.
Compels a body to perform a public duty it has refused.
States the legal position, without commanding anyone.
body.alt: Four orders. Certiorari quashes a decision already made. Prohibition stops a body from acting or continuing. Mandamus compels a body to perform a public duty it has refused. A declaration states the legal position without commanding anyone.

body.text: More than one can be sought together. Quashing a refusal often needs mandamus beside it, or the body simply refuses again.

body.q: The council never decided Bakri's application at all. Which order fits?
options: Certiorari, to quash the refusal
Mandamus, to compel a decision
Prohibition, to stop the council
body.why: There is no decision to quash. The complaint is inaction, and mandamus is the order that compels a public body to perform its duty.

sections.keypoint: Winning a review usually sends the decision back rather than replacing it.

body.text: Readers expect a successful review to hand them the licence. It usually does not.
The court quashes the decision and the matter returns to the body, which decides again, lawfully this time.
The body may reach the same result. If it does so on relevant grounds and after a fair procedure, that outcome stands.
There is authority for a court going further and substituting its own decision in an appropriate case. Treat that as exceptional and argue for it expressly rather than assuming it.
This follows from what review is for. The court polices how the power was used; it does not take the power over.

lessons.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 53. The remedies are the prerogative orders as applied in Malaysia.
lessons.verify: Read Order 53 itself for the leave requirement, the time limit and the sufficient-interest test, and check the current time limit rather than relying on a textbook.
