lessons.title: The limits on a discretion
lessons.summary: A power that says the Minister may do as he thinks fit is still a limited power. Four familiar failures turn a lawful-looking decision into an unlawful one, and none of them is about the decision being wrong.

sections.keypoint: A discretion has to be exercised for the purpose it was given for.
sections.h: A power given for a reason

body.text: A statute lets a local authority close a market for reasons of public health. The authority closes one to make room for a development it favours.
Nothing here is dishonest, and the decision may even be sensible. It is still unlawful.
A statutory power must be exercised for the purpose for which it was conferred. Using it to achieve some other object is an improper purpose, whatever the merits of that object.
body.source: Administrative law principle applied in Malaysia; see the grounds recognised under Order 53 review.

body.text: Find the purpose in the Act, not in what seems reasonable. That is what makes this a legality question rather than a merits one.

sections.keypoint: Considering the wrong things, or ignoring the right ones, is itself a ground.

body.text: The second failure is about the ingredients rather than the answer.
A decision-maker must consider what the statute makes relevant, and must not be influenced by what it does not.

A licensing authority refuses a permit partly because the applicant had criticised the council in the newspaper. That is an irrelevant consideration, and the refusal is open to challenge even if there were also good reasons.
The presence of a good reason does not always save a decision. Ask whether the irrelevant matter actually influenced the outcome.

sections.keypoint: A body that applies a rigid policy has stopped exercising the discretion it was given.

body.text: The third failure is the subtlest, and it looks like good administration.
A body adopts a policy so it treats like cases alike. Then it applies the policy to every case without looking at any of them.
A body entrusted with a discretion must not fetter it by applying a rigid rule. It may adopt a policy, but it must remain willing to consider an application that asks it to depart from that policy.
body.source: Administrative law principle applied in Malaysia.

body.text: So the answer to a policy is not that policies are unlawful. The answer is that this applicant was never actually considered.

body.prompt: An authority says: we never grant licences to applicants under 21, and we made no exception here. What is the ground?
options: Irrationality
Fettering the discretion
Procedural impropriety
body.reveal: Fettering. The authority may have a policy about age, but refusing to consider whether this case warrants departing from it means the statutory discretion was never exercised.

sections.keypoint: A clause saying a decision may not be questioned does not always mean what it says.
sections.h: Clauses that try to shut the court out

body.text: Parliament sometimes writes that a decision shall be final and shall not be called into question in any court.
Taken literally that ends review. Courts have not read such clauses literally.
The reasoning is narrow and worth stating precisely. The clause protects decisions the body had power to make. A decision made outside the power is not a decision of the kind the clause protects.
This is contested ground in Malaysia and the authorities repay careful reading. Do not assert that ouster clauses are simply ineffective — say why this decision falls outside what the clause covers.
Note also Article 121 in the background. How far Parliament may remove judicial power is a constitutional question, not merely one of construction.

lessons.source: The grounds of review as applied under Rules of Court 2012, Order 53; Federal Constitution, Article 121 for the constitutional dimension of ouster clauses.
lessons.verify: Check the current Malaysian authorities on ouster clauses before relying on this — the position has moved, and this lesson deliberately states the principle without asserting where the line now sits.
